maintopic: STATEMENT AS TO HOLIDAY FOR STAFF ON VICTORIA DAY
speechtext:
Some hon. members
having inquired whether the staff of the house would be given a holiday tomorrow, I have prepared the following statement.
There is no doubt that the staff of the House of Commons is entitled to a holiday tomorrow, but I have to consider the convenience of the members who intend to do some work in the building on that day. Such offices as the library, reading room and the post office, which are open on Sundays during the session, can hardly be closed. Mails will come regularly and will have to be sorted. Members preparing public statements might need to consult authorities or read newspapers. Apart from that all the clerical branches will be closed. As no doubt a great number of visitors will come into the building, we shall have to keep the constables and guides on duty. A couple of messengers will also have to work. The main dining room will be open until after luncheon, and the cafeteria will do business as usual. All the other members of the staff of the House of Commons, except the cleaners who will be employed from 6.30 to 8.30 and 9 a.m., will be on holiday. I am, however, in the hands of the house, and if hon. members decide that all the offices, except the constables, be closed, I will act accordingly.

maintopic: STATEMENT AS TO HOLIDAY FOR STAFF ON VICTORIA DAY

Agreed.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 253, to make provision with respect to forces of the United States of America when visiting Canada and with respect to the exercise of discipline and to the internal administration of such forces.
He said: During the war there were provisions under the War Measures Act facilitating the exercise of disciplinary and administrative powers by the commanders of United States forces that might be in Canada on the invitation of the Canadian government. Those provisions expired on April 1 when the orders in council, other than those appended to the so-called omnibus bill, were repealed. This is a bill to make provision for the exercise of some disciplinary and administrative powers by commanders of such United States forces as may be in Canada on the invitation of the Canadian government, but without in any way excluding the jurisdiction of our own courts of justice.

subtopic: CANADIANS LEAVING FOR YUGOSLAVIA-POSITION OF NATURALIZED CITIZEN LEAVING CANADA

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs):	Mr. Speaker,
on May 20 several questions were directed by hon. members to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and to me concerning the emigration to Yugoslavia of certain residents of Canada. As all the questions are related, the Prime Minister informed the house on May 21 that I would make a comprehensive statement on the subject.
The first suggestion that a group of Yugoslav nationals might leave Canada for Yugoslavia was made by the charge d'affaires of the Yugoslav legation in Ottawa in a letter, dated March 5, 1946. In this letter he stated that there were a number of Yugoslav nationals who wished to return to Yugoslavia when transportation facilities became available. He also raised the question of export permits for various Canadian products on behalf of the nationals concerned. The charge d'affaires was subsequently advised of the export regulations then in force.
In June, 1946, passports were granted to four Canadians of Yugoslav origin for the purpose of proceeding to Yugoslavia. The passports were granted subsequent to a written request from the charge d'affaires of the Yugoslav

Emigration
legation in which he stated that the applicants wished to proceed to Yugoslavia to make arrangements for certain Yugoslav nationals or Canadian citizens of Yugoslav descent who "were planning to return to Yugoslavia for the purpose of lending their skill and assistance in the reconstruction of the country."
Subsequent to the return of these persons to Canada a good deal appeared in the Yugo-slav-Canadian press about the return of Yugoslavs and Canadians of Yugoslav descent to Yugoslavia and it appears that funds were collected in connection with the proposed emigration.
In regard to the export of capital the regulations of the foreign exchange control board provide as hon. members know, that persons leaving Canada for permanent residence elsewhere are provided with sufficient foreign exchange to pay their passages and reasonable expenses en route. They are allowed to export personal and household effects, and their remaining cash assets up to a maximum of $25,000 each are transferable in Canadian funds.
A proposal was made by the Yugoslav charge d'affaires under which the resources of the emigrants, within the policy stated above, would be pooled through a central organization known as the Council of Canadian South Slavs. This body, instead of withdrawing the funds from Canada, would use them to make bulk purchases in Canada of goods suitable to trades in which the emigrants would engage upon their return to Yugoslavia.
This proposal was approved and bank accounts were established by the Council of Canadian South Slavs under the supervision of the foreign exchange control board. Although up-to-date figures are not available at present, deposits to the accounts have amounted to approximately $1,000,000.
In this connection export permits have been granted by the Department of Trade and Commerce for the export of material from Canada to Yugoslavia to the amount of $345,918. Some permits were granted to individuals direct; other permits were granted to Canadian manufacturers who apparently received orders for direct shipment.
Settlers' effects are not under export permit control. A farmer leaving Canada, therefore, would be free to take his farming equipment without the necessity of an export permit and, in a similar way, a mechanic would be free to take the tools of his trade. Undoubtedly the total value of settlers' effects would be considerable, but it is difficult to estimate the exact value involved.
It is also difficult to estimate the total number of persons leaving Canada under the auspices of the Council of Canadian South Slavs since passports would be applied for by the individuals concerned, if they are Canadians, and Yugoslavs would travel on Yugoslav passports. There is, of course, no regulation or law which prevents a Canadian or an alien leaving Canada of his own free will. The legal position of an alien leaving Canada is governed by the Immigration Act which provides that an alien acquires Canadian domicile "only by having his domicile for at least five years in Canada after having been landed therein". He loses his domicile by "voluntarily residing out of Canada with the present intention of making his permanent home out of Canada and not for a mere special or temporary purpose."
Thus a Yugoslav citizen, regardless of the length of time he has lived in Canada, will lose his right to reenter Canada if he goes to Yugoslavia with the intention of making his permanent home in Yugoslavia. Should he change his mind and wish to reenter Canada, he would have no right to reenter Canada and would have to apply for admission as any other prospective immigrant.
Moreover, if he should be readmitted to Canada, he could not count his previous stay in Canada for the acquisition of Canadian domicile. In order to become a citizen of Canada, he would, after his return, have to remain in Canada for five years.
The legal position of a Canadian citizen by naturalization leaving Canada is governed by sections 20 and 21 of the Canadian Citizenship Act. Section 20 reads in part as follows: "A Canadian citizen, other than a natural-born Canadian citizen . . . ceases to be a Canadian citizen if he resides outside Canada for a period of at least six consecutive years," subject to various provisos. Section 21 provides inter alia for cancellation of citizenship by order-in-council if a naturalized citizen "out of Canada has shown himself by act or speech to be disaffected or disloyal to His Majesty."
It is important to note that a warning appears at the back of the current Canadian passport, which reads as follows:
Canadian citizens by naturalization certificate or citizenship certificate should bear in mind that unless under the laws of the state to which they originally belonged or by the provision of a treaty, they have ceased to be subjects of that state, their certificates have no effect within its boundaries nor can the good offices of His Majesty's representatives be extended to them there.
If. therefore, any Canadian citizen by naturalization who goes to Yugoslavia is,
Newfoundland

under Yugoslav law, a citizen of Yugoslavia, the Canadian government will not be able to grant him any measure of protection as long as he remains in Yugoslavia.
The group, which is now assembled in Montreal, have satisfied the various regulations applicable to their movement to Yugoslavia both in regard to themselves and to goods purchased by them. No doubt they are aware of their possible loss of status under Canadian law but they are free to go to Yugoslavia or to any other country if they so wish.
On May 21 the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) asked whether I would take steps to see that the Canadian passports carried by the expatriate Yugoslavs now in process of returning to their homeland be protected in such a way as to prevent their alteration or transference to other persons, and ensure that each Canadian passport issued to this group will be easily identifiable on its reentry to Canada. I can assure the hon. member that every effort will be made to guard against the misuse of these Canadian passports.
Allegations have been made in the press that improper methods have been used to persuade residents of Canada to return to Yugoslavia or to contribute to the funds which have been raised to finance the return of other residents of Canada. Should any evidence come to hand as to the methods used in these or any other cases which would warrant action by the government, it will not hesitate to take such action.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, May 22, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Muskoka-Ontario) and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.
Mr. W. CHESTER S. McLURE (Queens): Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege last night of moving the adjournment of the debate. I want to say for the benefit of hon. members
83166-216$

that I have waited for some considerable time for a member from my province to speak on behalf of that province. As they have not seen fit to do so I believe it is my duty to say a few words at this time. I feel that if any member from my province had spoken what he would have said would have been more favourable to the government than what I am about to say.
After I moved adjournment of the debate last night some of my friends on both sides of the house said to me, "Well, we will hear tomorrow all about that car ferry, freight and truck traffic, transportation and the nonfulfilment of the confederation pact." At first I felt that this was a rather embarrassing suggestion, but on second thought I realize it is a compliment, whether or not it was intended as such. If I had time-

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would ask hon. members to moderate their voices. It is nearly impossible to hear the hon. member who has the floor. I suggest that those who have important conversations to carry on might use the lobby.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Or let them go to their rooms, Mr. Speaker, and have their usual sleep. If I had time this house would surely hear about the government's neglect in fulfilment of our confederation pact, but another time is coming, and before this house rises, even if it is in September or October, I shall have my say on that subject. I am not afraid to demand from this government or any other government or any other party the rights that belong to my province as a province.
I have noticed, Mr. Speaker, as you have noticed, that as soon as hon. members rise to speak in this debate a great many members hike for the nearest exit as if somebody had called out "All ashore that's going ashore". I have kept a partial register of this and I have found that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had a full house, and in my humble opinion he deserved it, whether he pleased them or otherwise. But as hon. members on different sides began to debate the budget the attendance petered out from a full house to a score of deuces and one queen. I have kept a register of attendance when the hon. members were speaking and on a great many occasions there was barely a quorum in the house. But what is the difference, Mr. Speaker? We are all speaking to Hansard, to our constituents, so after all we are all on a par. As I look at the government side today I am grateful for a better attendance than most 
hon. members have had, and I would say thank you to them for that. I will say this, that if there were no Hansard, reporters in this house I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I could fill this chamber in the next ten minutes -if there was no record to go to the country of what I should say-and that is true of a great many others.
In this budget debate I have not missed one sitting of the house. I have listened to all the speeches on the maritimes except the one delivered by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and I could not help being absent on that occasion; I was called out of the house. Some of the speeches I am not in a position to understand fully, and ,1 regret that very much indeed. When hon. members speak in that classical language, French, unless they go slowly and carefully, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) do, I am at a loss to understand what they say. While I was born in a French settlement in Prince Edward Island, known as North Rustico-and I was proud to be born in that, settlement-I always held it against the French people there that they wanted to learn English but we were not privileged to learn French. However, the other day on happening to meet one of the French members of the redistribution committee I interpreted to him what I wanted to make known with regard to Queens county. I said this to him, "Ne touchez pas Queens."
During this debate, and especially within the last couple of days, I have felt elated, Mr. Speaker, that the maritimes are being recognized, so well recognized that I am almost envious that we have not a by-election pending in the province of Prince Edward Island. When the government realize that they have a long overdue by-election on their hands they seem to sit up and take notice, to warm up to the fact that the maritimes are a part of Canada. But I do not give the entire credit to the by-election. I believe that hon. members who have spoken so ably on the unfulfilled obligations of the government to the neglected maritimes have exerted a great deal of influence. I refer to such hon. members as the member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black), the hon. member for Colehester-Hants (Mr. Stanfield), the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), the hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough (Mr. Kirk), and there have been a great many others. I didi hope, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges), with all his eloquence, would have spoken on the rights of the maritimes in this debate. I do wish to say that it afforded me real pleasure when the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MAY 23, 1947
The Budget-Mr. McLure
MacNicol), a constituency of that great province of Ontario, climaxed his efforts by his interest and factual information regarding the neglected maritimes of this dominion. It was a grand and glorious feeling for me when he spoke about the best bit of red earth in the world, my province. It was an assurance to me also that my efforts to keep the island on the map have not been in vain. All this, Mr. Speaker, is a preamble to the subject that is before us for debate at this time, one that is important to us all whether we are in private or political life, and that is the subject of the budget.
In introducing the budget on April 29 the Minister of Finance informed the house that it was his first. Political history records the fact that it is either the making or the breaking of the man who first delivers the budget. At this time I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance on playing first fiddle. Since his debut in political life seven years ago the hon. gentleman has played many parts in government. He played second fiddle to the ex-minister of finance (Mr. Ilsley); second fiddle to the ex-minister of defence, Hon. J. L. Ralston, and to another ex-minister, General A. G. L. McNaughton. Then through the strategy of the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Case), he became minister of defence. On Tuesday, April 29, we found him calling the tune and playing first fiddle. At that time it was interesting to note how the Prime Minister smiled upon him as he called him to the second fiddle seat in the front row, and when the Minister of Finance in his address would draw a long bow with a high note how the Prime Minister beamed upon his protege with the nicest of Virginian smiles!
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance told us that a great day is coming. What the people want is the present day to be great. They are not willing to buy futures even on a 29 per cent profit margin. A few days prior to the minister delivering his budget speech I looked at a picture of him in the Globe and Mail. I do not believe he had a moustache at that time. There I saw a man in comfortable attire, shirtsleeves rolled up to the biceps, earning his $18,000 annual indemnity by the sweat of his noble brow. It reminded me of the words of a great British Prime Minister who said, "sweat and tears" *-sweat for the Minister of Finance but tears for the taxpayers of Canada.
According to the minister he laboured hard and well to make us believe that his first budget held out more money for all, higher wages for all, higher profits for all, lower taxes for all, lower prices for all, higher production for all industry with floor and ceiling prices to protect producers and consumers. Oh, what a hope! But notwithstanding all this clanging of tambourines and idealistic verbiage, when the searchlight is turned on the budget it reveals at the same time the nigger in the woodpile of hope for better things. By this budget will come stifling of private enterprise with less production, more jobless men-and it is reported we have thirty thousand of them in the maritimes at the present time-more discontent and general dissatisfaction throughout the entire country.
Having listened attentively to the minister's budget from the first to the last I wondered who prepared it-I knew who delivered it, and in my opinion it was exceptionally well delivered. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part in this debate, even at this late stage. I have had the privilege of listening to others, and in what I shall say I shall try not to repeat what others have said.
The last few minutes, when we have had to listen to the woes and the wails and the painting of that dismal future for Canada, have been most painful. I do not think anything can be more destructive than the wails and woes such as we have heard from the hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. McLure).
Before approaching my main item, may I compliment the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) who painted such a. rosy picture of his constituency. From his speech one could tell that nature was close to his heart. I am sure the people of his constituency are behind him, heart and soul, when he tries to do something for them.
May I express a vote of thanks, too, to the hon. member for North York (Mr. Smith) who, along with others has been trying to bring about dominion-provincial meetings so that his constituency might receive the benefit therefrom.
I should like also to compliment that grand old man from Brandon (Mr. Matthews), the daddy of the house. When I heard him making his colourful speech I knew he had his people at heart. No wonder he has retained his seat for such a long time.
I would compliment, too, the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) upon his fine speech.
Today I speak as a back-bencher, one who is not in the $18,000 brackets which have

The Budget-Mr. Sinnott
been mentioned. I am going to speak on my own behalf, not on behalf of the party; and in doing so I shall express my own opinion. I shall not be over-critical of any party in the house, for the simple reason that as a back-bencher, whether my views are good or bad, I do not suppose they will be taken anyway.
The former minister of finance worked under terrific strain during wartime, and he has now given way to a younger man, a man who must work very hard, with his shirt sleeves rolled up, as was pointed out by an earlier speaker. Having been reeve of a municipality for a number of years I can join hands with him in my knowledge of the terrific strain to which he must have been subjected in carrying out his financing. I maintain that the whole process of financing is based on a system of debt. This afternoon I shall attempt to make my opinions as clear as possible. As chairman of a school board I found that the board had to borrow money from the bank to carry on its year's activities, and had to pay a terrific amount of interest on the amount it borrowed. The municipalities, in turn, had to borrow money from the bank to carry on their activities for the year. Provincial and dominion governments must do the same thing.
Just to show the inconsistencies in connection with getting money, let me point out one or two things. To get money when you need it and to get it when you do not need it are two different things. The first year I was reeve of a municipality of 4,000 people our credit stood at $8,000. We were in dire need of money at that time-that was back in 1936-but we were refused it, because it was said that our credit was not good. It was pointed out to us that some of our taxes were outstanding. We had only $8,000 to operate our schools, for which the sum of $30,000 was required. After seven or eight years of good financing we reduced the municipal debt by $229,000. We bought a drag line and other modern road equipment, and also built 400 miles of road. In the last year we could have got $50,000 credit at the bank, but we did not need it then. What I have stated illustrates that money is plentiful when it is not required, but when one is in dire need of it he cannot have it.
Anyone who will read the little red book will see that I am set down as an implement dealer. It happened that I was following that occupation for a few months prior to my coming to Ottawa. But during the greater part of my life I have been farming, and it is on behalf of the farmers I should like to say a few words today.
There are two classes of farmers. There is the grain grower, and there is the other farmer who produces live stock in addition to his grain crops. I have not much sympathy for the man who is just growing grain, because I know that on the western prairies they simply sow their seed in the spring and take off their crops in the fall, year in and year out, with the result that the land becomes lighter and blows away. They are robbers of the soil. The men whom I want to defend are the dairy farmers and the hog raisers. These men really work for a living, milking their cows, raising hogs, and so on. They must farm 365 dajrs in the year. They cannot just pull out in the fall, go to California and return in the spring-they must stay on the job. The animals must be fed in the morning, the cows must be milked, then fed again at dinner time and at night. The daily chores of such a farmer run from six in the morning until ten o'clock at night.
I have a letter here from the secretary treasurer of the municipality in which I reside which shows the extent of the benefits derived from the dominion-provincial conference. This municipality is going to get six mills on the general assessment. School taxes vary from 35 mills to 61 mills, and in most cases it has been a great help. In the case of a property worth $3,000, there will be a reduction of $18 in the school taxes alone, or approximately 30 per cent.
An hon. member has mentioned Mr. Krug. I have a letter from him which reads in part:
Your ideas of using the Bank of Canada to finance public indebtedness and the private banks to finance private activities are similar to my own views.
Let us not have any more of this funny money story we hear so much about. The Bank of Canada should be used for the benefit of the people of Canada. Some people will say, "Oh, something for nothing." This is the funny money story that crops up and which we hear so much about. Let me say here and now that it would be the same kind of money as I hold here in my hand.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have but one purpose in taking part in the present budget debate. I am compelled to voice the intense disappointment of the citizens of my riding and Canadians in all walks of life at the financial sleight-of-hand displayed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his first budget address. To say' that the minister made a clever speech is unhappily true. His voice was strong even though his arguments were a bit weak. The applause from the back benches of the Liberal party was vociferous if a bit forced. The congratulatory press releases of the next day covered up the obvious and growing decay of government statemanship with clever facades of impressive statistics.
The minister's speech reminded me of nothing so much as a conducted tour of a district under the arrangement of the local chamber of commerce. Such tours invariably show the credulous tourist the respectable scenes of 
the community. He is shown the great public and industrial buildings, the main streets and the landscaped homes of the thriving local aristocracy, all telling the story of material success and accumulating wealth. But the guide shields his visitors from even a glimpse of the local slums, from the unkempt and undernourished children and from the garrets of poverty on the other side of the tracks by whose degradation the outward glittering facade is usually able to be maintained. Such a guide was Canada's Minister of Finance in his economic report to the nation three weeks ago. To the House of Commons he said, and I quote from page 2543 of Hansard of April 29:
Today we see a Canada enjoying a degree of prosperity never exceeded in living memory. We look forward to a year of high production and incomes. Indeed, we would appear to have ample excuse for self-satisfaction and easy optimism.
Those were the minister's words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go on and read what I said after that; read the whole text.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have read it. I do not doubt that is the view to be seen on the minister's side of the tracks. To his sightseeing colleagues on the treasury benches such a picture is reasonable, because the federal books shows an apparent surplus of $352 million in government operations for the fiscal year just concluded.
The annual reports of big business to shareholders show that industrial companies have had a similar money experience: from the 1946 balance sheet of Monarch Knitting Company, showing a 309 per cent increase in net profits over 1945; from Orange Crush Company, a 448 per cent increase; from Building Products Company, a 256 per cent increase; from Moirs' Chocolates, a 226 per cent increase; from International Paper, a 265 per cent increase; from major corporations everywhere, equally staggering reports of golden harvests in practically all lines of business, thanking the government no doubt for past favours, but holding out sticky hands for more and yet more concessions by way of relaxed price controls, of bigger export guarantees, double depreciation, lower income tax rates, and removal of checks on excess profits.
And the minister, having heard the perpetual clamour of the lobbyist for bigger and better profits, and perhaps planning strategy for the inevitable election, the only type of planing which has merit in the eyes of laissez-faire governments, trots out his carefully groomed budget for our inspection. Well, let us look at it. Here is his forecast for the next year:

The Budget-Mr. Probe
Sales tax up $27 million; excise duties and other excise taxes up $13 million-thus far an increase of $40 million. Definitely no relief there to the people who pay such taxes.
Excess profits taxes cut by $279 million. There is a nice fat incentive melon to the overworked coupon clippers.
Personal income taxes down $70 million, with no change in previously announced exemptions. There is another load cut off the weary shoulders of income taxpayers, with tax relief given, as usual, under capitalism, in inverse ratio to need.
Of course the minister informed the house that over half the people of Canada are now receiving so little pay that they pay no income tax anyway; and that in spite of an exemption figure which is below the cost of living. Families in the low income brackets do not cheer the 1947 budget.
But a few of those who have better than average incomes do quite well by themselves. Not the single man getting $800 yearly, whose need for incentive to produce more is valued at $6 for the next year since he will save only $6 next year on income tax. That saving will not give him a net balance after the rising costs of room rent, food and clothing are considered.
But a single man now getting $3,000 yearly will have $173 annual tax relief. He needs $173 to whip up his incentive. And one getting $10,000 a year will have $785 more relief than in 1946. It seems to take a bigger bonus in the view of the Minister of Finance to create an incentive to the $10,000 a year bachelor to work for that brave new world!
On the minister's side of the tracks such lopsided tax relief is not only fair but necessary! A married man with two children will, if he is now getting $150 a month, save $10 a year. Remember, the Minister of Finance puts such a man in 'the upper crust of Canada's salary scale. Maybe fear of starvation should be ample incentive for such a man! For him a tax reduction of eighty-three cents a month, to lay away for the rising cost of shoes, or enough to pay the increased cost of less than half the milk his children need

if they could afford to eat those things they should be eating.
Of course a married man with wages of $250 a month gets $83 a year cut from his income tax. or enough to allow him to pay his landlord $7 a month more rent, now that rental ceilings have conveniently risen to absorb the tax relief. You can trust a good landlord to cooperate!
The married man with two children and a salary of $10,000 a year gets approximately $2 a day relief from his tax burden.
And so it goes. The higher your income, the higher is the value the Minister of Finance puts on incentive. The higher your income, and the less your need, the greater the relief from income tax. To continue to quote from Scripture, as has been done so conveniently this afternoon, "For whomsoever hath, to him shall be given,"-by all versions.
And what about the minister's plans for increased incentives to the corporations whose profits I quoted a moment ago? Where in the past fiscal year corporation and excess profits taxes of $688 million were taken away from the industrialists, next year will see only $470 million returned to the people of Canada from this source. A cool incentive of $218 million to big business! Not a bad year's work in the lobbies for free enterprise! The minister is helping to reconstruct post-war capitalism with a vengeance, and as always, at the expense of the underfed and the under privileged! For a single year, Canadian corporations get tax reductions amounting to more than six years federal payments of old age pensions at the current rate. Nothing stingy about that scale of relief for rugged industrialists! But the needy pensioner still waits for government action! And still the Tories are not satisfied! The incentives I have mentioned are still not enough for the family compact!
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell). in his role as spokesman for the Progressive Conservative party on the budget, demanded that the government take steps to return government interest rates from their present three per cent to the good old five and six per cent of the Tory-dominated finance rates of world war I. Strange how the Conservatives babble away incessantly about government economies, and then one of their most respected front benchers demands interest rates that would raise Canada's self-imposed subsidy to parasitic money-lenders by another $437 million yearly. This one request bv the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario would build up a $875 million present annually from Canada to the great financial institutions and the so-called middle class pensioners for whom my hon. member the financial critic for the Progressive Conservative pleads so eloquently. I wonder whether he will ever plead as sincerely for the expenditure of an equal amount of Canadian money for a universal old age pension scheme for all Canadians, to include those who live on the other side of the tracks as well as his beloved middle-class pensioners. They have to face the facts of life more insecurely equipped than do the coupon clippers who would make every day a day for Christmas giving to themselves.
The Budget-Mr. Probe

I regret to state, Mr. Speaker, that, in my view, so far as the post-war period is concerned the economic action of the government has been one of gradually yielding to the wishes and the policies of the Conservative party. The Liberals, yes, and even the Tories on occasion, in debate and in their election literature so often talk the language of a planned economy as advocated by the C.C.F. They do this on the hustings because they are astute enough to know that economic planning is what Canada must have and what Canadians will vote for, but after every election to office the great betrayal is shameless and persistent. This budget gives relief to the rich once more, and it leaves at least the majority of Canadians worse off than before by its failure to eliminate or reduce hidden taxes, the more vicious because they are concealed taxes. I refer to the sales, customs and excise taxes. In his address the minister said that over half the Canadians were too poor to pay income tax; yet these same poor people bear the heaviest tax rate of all our citizens, with the hidden indirect tax of eight per cent, the sales tax and the excise tax. For those who need tax relief most the minister has done nothing in the budget. Not only are these low income families unable to get the meagre benefits of income tax reduction because they have no taxable income, but this coming year the full impact of rising rents, higher costs of food and of clothing, the unnecessary removal of the various subsidies on milk, butter, coal and so on play havoc with the pay cheque of the family.
Let me state this in another way. It is primary economics under any modern government that is not a malevolent dictatorship for public revenues to be levied in accordance with ability to pay, and that the greater the tax needed, the more steeply graduated must be the rates. No such economic policy is at work in the minister's present tax structure; in fact it is quite the reverse. Even in the field of corporation tax the Liberal policy is content to levy a uniform rate on great and small operators alike. Where does the accepted principle of ability to pay rest in the minister's calculation, in this instance?
By the British North America Act of 1867 the powers of provincial governments were limited to the right to collect direct taxes such as those levied on incomes or estates. These taxes cannot be concealed in the cost of living or in the cost of production. In their payment the taxpayer is always acutely conscious of the fact that he is paying taxes and of the amount that he is being taxed. By the same act the dominion government was empowered to levy either direct taxes such as the income fix, or indirect taxes such as the customs,
l"Mr. Probe.]
sales or excise tax. Until 1917, during world war I, the dominion remained out of the field of direct taxation, confining its tax powers to those which the producer or importer could usually pass on to the ultimate consumer by concealing the tax in the price tag.
These taxes being hidden in the price tag, were not so glaringly evident to the consumer and, being unknown taxes, were not unpopular. He became critical of the income tax only when his income became taxable, but accepted the more regressive sales tax because he was unaware that, regardless of how low his income, heavy taxes were, in fact, being charged against him, but concealed in the prices of the necessities he bought.
As late as 1930, one-third of all taxes in Canada were of the hidden variety, and just barely one-fifteenth of all taxes were levied on income or inheritance; or, in other words, only one-fifteenth of municipal, provincial and federal taxes were based on ability to pay. It is through this economic sleight-of-hand of dominion ministers of finance, by which they weave sales taxes, excise taxes and customs duties into the cost of living that they pick the pockets of the low-income citizen of Canada.
Every time he buys a can of corned beef for his lunch pail, or the overall for his back, or the paper with which he shapes his smoke, or the tools with which he earns his meagre income-tax-free pay cheque, or when he turns on a light switch to find his weary bed at night, this consumer, who is free from direct tax, still pays a more onerous tax than does his neighbour in the fashionable suburb.
When he buys soles to repair the shoes of his children, or he pays for the cloth his wife uses to patch the holes in the inferior quality clothes that business ethics condone, he pays generous profits to unbridled enterprise (plus customs duty on the imported portions), plus the eight per cent sales tax to the Minister of Finance, plus a 50 per cent to 75 per cent collection fee on the tax, also concealed in the extra mark-up, and too often a 1-J per cent to 2 per cent per month finance charge due to recent sickness or unemployment having caused bills to accumulate.
Even the chocolate bar and the pop bottle pay their regressive tax of 20 per cent to 40 per cent to help create the surplus of the Minister of Finance. The soda-fountain courtships of Canada's glowing-cheeked adolescents are halted till the tax collector gets his two cents a bottle. With the price difference between the drugstore soda and the barroom beer so little, it is small wonder that I have had nearly three hundred letters from youth groups of Regina and elsewhere draw-

The Budget-Mr. Probe
ing attention to the moral danger implied in the minister's sales and excise tax policy, as well as to the disproportionate share of Canada's tax burden charged against the teenage habits of our youngsters. It is refreshing to me that Canadian youth is more keenly alert to the injustice of regressive taxation policies, and more vociferous in protest, than are adult citizens who may be below the income tax exemption; for the latter, quite aware that they pay little or none of the direct income taxes to which their better-off neighbours are liable, remain complacent about the hidden taxes, even while they are bewildered as to the real reason why their wages never quite stay ahead of living expenses.
I will make a wager with the Minister of Finance that if he would make it compulsory for the next six months for every sales tag to show the amount of the price covered by hidden indirect tax, either he would be compelled to bring in a proper sales tax in the next budget, or the Liberal party would go out of existence at the next election.
But so long as the tax may be hidden from the consumer, sufficiently to prevent widespread political repercussions, the degree of impact of the tax burden is to the Liberals of as small concern as it was to the despotic Bourbons of France 200 years ago.
A sales tax that nets the government eight per cent at the point of collection becomes a tax of 12 to 14 per cent to the consumer by the time the wholesaler and retailer have added their mark-up. So that when the government estimates receipts from excise taxes -and duties of $490 million; customs duties of $230 million, and sales tax of $325 million, these hidden taxes totalling $1,045 million will actually cost Canadian consumers, because of the mefEceney of collection procedure, from $1,500 to $1,800 million for 1947. This is one important view of Canada's budget which the minister neglected to show our people, and which I feel must be shown to complete the scene.
Since levy of indirect taxes is not based on ability to pay, Canadians will in 1947, for each family of five persons, pay an average of $600 to $720 in higher cost of living, due to indirect taxation, with the greatest tax impact on the small wage consumer. From any married wage-earner this takes away in hidden taxes several times what the government pays back in family allowances, more decently to feed, clothe and shelter his children. The sales tax becomes a tax burden in inverse ratio to the income of the family.
In his failure to lighten the heavy hidden load of sales tax, the Minister of Finance has
been grossly unfeeling and unfair in his responsibilities of office. His loyal colleague, the would-be Liberal premier of Saskatchewan, the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) indulges in spasms of double talk on this subject. In Saskatchewan, in days that were happier from the point of view of the political aspirations of the hon. member for Rosthern, a Liberal government once imposed a two per cent sales tax in the name of education. Thi3 tax, despite the limited tax resources of my province, has twice been modified since the C.C.F. government headed by Premier Douglas took office in 1944. Out in Saskatchewan the hon. member for Rosthern has waxed eloquent for the complete removal of a tax which his Liberal colleagues of recent memory themselves imposed. Then in Ottawa the same hon. gentleman, blandly or blindly or both, supports the continuance of taxation far more regressive and at least seven times as costly to the consumer, by a government having constitutional power to secure revenue from all manner of means denied to one of the poorest provinces in the Dominion of Canada. What an obvious faux pas in logic by a would-be premier.
And note how the other Liberal member from Saskatchewan tries to sugar over the indefensible position of the federal government. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who is, in my opinion, one of the cleverest debaters of the Liberal party, speaking on May 12 highlighted his party's spoken promises in contrast to their fiscal deeds in these words, as reported at page 2961 of Hansard:
And I might go further and say that all forma of indirect taxation in Canada today were brought into being in the first instance by a Conservative government. It is true that some have been maintained in part by the Liberal governments which succeeded those Conservative administrations, but in only one instance has there been an increase in one of these indirect taxes. That was the instance referred to a moment ago by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), when he said I might have gone a little further. Yes, I might have gone a little further and said the sales tax was increased by the present government in the budget of 1936, in order to take care of the costs which had been placed against the people of this country while the previous government was in power. The intention of the government was-
These are the salient words.
-to reduce that taxation, just as it had done in other instances. But, Mr. Speaker, we have been through a war which lasted for six years. During those six years the cost of carrying on government was greatly increased, _ with the result that up to the present time it has not been found possible to reduce that particular form of taxation.

The Budget-Mr. Probe

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that not true, that we had gone through a war?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Liberal government put the tax I refer to back on again in 1936 or 1937. We have here in the speech of the Minister of Agriculture just another example of the Liberal pot calling the Tory kettle black. The record of both Liberal and Conservative governments since world war I emphatically belies the sincerity of speakers of both the old-line parties. In this debate, both Liberals and Conservatives say they have a genuine concern to lower regressive indirect taxation, which, not being based on ability to pay, is doubly and trebly unjust to low-income Canadians. But their actions, when they were in power after 1920, give the lie to these professions of concern.
Here is my proof for saying that neither Liberals nor Conservatives have a record in office which can be trusted in the field of regressive taxation. I am going to give figures from the Canada Year Book, 1938, at page 836. On this page there appears a statement of sales tax changes from 1920 to 1938.
In 1920, on May 19, there was placed on the statutes a domestic sales tax of one per cent on sales by manufacturers, one per cent on sales by wholesalers and one per cent on importation. In June of that year the rate on sales by manufacturers to retailers or consumers was raised to two per cent and the import sales tax was raised to two per cent on importations by retailers or by consumers; that is, by the end users.
In 1921-and we are coming now to the government of the present Prime Minister- 1J per cent was the rate on sales by manufacturers to wholesalers, It per cent on sales by wholesalers, three per cent on sales by manufacturers to retailers or consumers, except lumber, upon which the tax was two per cent on all domestic sales; and the import tax had gone up proportionately to 2 j per cent to manufacturers and wholesalers, and four per cent to the retailer or consumer.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I
correct a slight error. In 1921 the Liberal government was elected in December.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank the minister for the correction. We will then admit that these figures I have given thus far are during the Conservative regime, because in the next year, in 1922, when the present Prime Minister was in office, the sales tax, which was 1} per cent under the Tory regime, or the Union regime the year before, now became 2i per cent on sales by manufacturers fMr. Probe.]
to wholesalers, 2J per cent on sales by wholesalers, and 4j per cent on sales by manufacturers to retailers or consumers, except lumber, on which the tax was now raised just one per cent on all domestic sales; and the import figure now had risen to six per cent on importations by retailers and consumers.
In 1924 it had become six per cent on sales by manufacturers or producers, with three per cent on a restricted list, and six per cent on importations. In April, 1924-I presume there was an election in sight; in fact, there were several in the next two years, in 1925 and 1926-the list was reduced somewhat: five per cent on sales by manufacturers and five per cent on importations. That lasted for three years, until 1927, after the Meighen regime, and now the present Prime Minister was back on the throne. It was reduced in 1927 to four per cent, reduced in 1928 to three per cent, reduced in 1929 to two per cent, and reduced in 1930 to one per cent. He had brought it back to where it was just before he came into office.
In 1931 my hon. friends under the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett took office, and immediately swatted it up to a nice four per cent on sales by manufacturers and four per cent on importations. In 1932 it went to six per cent in each case, and in 1933 a distinction was made in the case of light articles manufactured by the blind, which were rated at half the tax for other manufactures. There was no change until 1936 when my Liberal friends came into office again, and in 1936, at the time when regressive taxation had its most burning effect on the pocket-books of low-income and relief people, the Liberal government raised that sales tax from six per cent to eight per cent on sales by manufacturers, and eight per cent on imports.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the statements that have been made in this House of Commons by members speaking for the government, and by members speaking for the Conservative party, are belied by the actions of their governments when they were in office.
My remarks at this time have been confined to regressive taxation; but, before closing, I should like to record my support of the remarks made on the budget by the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. McKay), who spoke on the irrigation needs of my area; the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), who dealt with a more progressive trade policy, and the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton), who analysed the implications in regard to agriculture contained

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
in this budget. At some other time I hope to refer to the record of the government in the field of public, housing.
In closing, I must pay tribute to the leader of the C.C.F. party, the statesman representative from Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), for his broad knowledge of both domestic and international matters and, above all, for his unflinching adherence to decent social and economic principles. Were my leader's principles implemented by a Canadian government acting for all sections and classes of our citizens instead of for a privileged Canadian economic aristocracy, the C.C.F. subamend'-ment moved by the hon. member on Tuesday, May 6, would have been unnecessary. That amendment was in these words:
That the following words be added to the amendment:
"(d) fail to raise the income tax exemption levels; and
(e) fail to make any provision for the more than half of our population who are compelled to live on incomes below the present exemption levels."

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my principal reason for participating in this debate this afternoon is to establish clearly and definitely the position of the Social Credit group in relation to the Progressive Conservative amendment and also in relation to the C.C.F. subamendment. In doing so, I shall present concrete reasons for the stand we intend to take. Before proceeding to do that, however, there are certain other observations I should like to make.
The budget debate opens the door wide and presents an opportunity for the discussion of a broad category of subjects. We have heard some speakers deal almost entirely with matters of local consequence; that is, those directly affecting their own constituencies. We have had many speeches dealing with matters of a national character, and also many referring to the general international situation. At first I was tempted to concentrate my remarks upon two or three matters which are the primary concern of my own constituency. While sorely tempted, for example, to devote my full forty minutes to one major local problem, namely the Red Deer post office and customs building and the inadequacy of service resulting from the deplorable condition of that building, I shall reluctantly defer consideration of that matter. But should it be necessary later, during this very session I shall devote forty minutes to that subject and direct my remarks to the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand), the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). I hope I may not have to do that. Then, too, it is difficult for
me to resist the temptation to devote my full forty minutes to a second vigorous protest [DOT] against the contemplated joint action on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railways, with the blessing of the board of transport commissioners and the governor general in council, to abandon &L) miles of railway in the Red Deer district, and thus, among other things, reduce land values in that area, virtually ruin several villages and hamlets, adversely affect our mail service, increase the cost of grain, live stock, coal and lumber marketing, contribute toward unemployment, cripple certain small private businesses, and provide cause for increases in municipal taxation. My opinions and the opinions of those directly affected by this retrograde action will certainly be made known to this house before the day of prorogation arrives.
I should like now, Mr. Speaker, to refer to just one or two speeches which have been made in this house during the past few days. First, I should like to refer to page 3310 of Hansard. The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) was speaking at the time. I am not referring to this because he happened to be the speaker but because he seemed to reflect a view held by a great many members on the other side of the house. Referring to dominion-provincial relations, the hon. member said:
In a country as great as Canada, so immensely rich in lands, forests, fisheries, minerals and other natural resources, with a small population of not quite 13,000,000 inhabitants, we do not want, as was suggested by the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleehe, to go back to the conditions which prevailed in 1921, for example, or in 1930, or even to the conditions which prevailed from 1937 to 1939, because, if we remember well, the last economic crisis was sunk in the rivers of blood of the last great war. We do not want to see again in this country thousands of Canadians on direct relief, or living in a state next to starvation merely because of the lack of proper provision in the constitution of this country, or the lack of collaboration between federal and provincial powers, or, in other words, because of the blindness, the short-sightedness and the foolishness of men.
Let me assure the hon. member, to start with, that I for one certainly do not wish to see those conditions occur again; but I think in the latter part of that statement, instead of saying "or in other words", he should have said simply "because of the blindness, the short-sightedness and the foolishness of men." The thing I want to point out is this.
I fully recognize that we desire a complete understanding and working agreement between the dominion and provincial authorities. In my opinion it is certainly necessary that we develop a proper concept of a working federal democracy, with the restatement and redefi-
The Budget-Mr. Shaw

nition of rights, authorities and responsibilities of all governments. But-and I lay emphasis upon this-if the hon. member for Bonaven-ture and those who think as he does with respect to this matter believe that the mere transfer of authority from the provinces to the dominion will, in itself, prevent unemployment, prevent business stagnation, or prevent another war, then I say the hon. gentleman is in for a rude awakening. I assert that with that we must have certain fundamental changes in those economic and financial policies which, as they now stand, contribute to unemployment, relief, crushing taxation and debt, trade wars and military wars. It does not matter who administers the dose of poison; the results will be the same in either case.
A number of members from the maritime provinces have laid a good deal of emphasis upon conditions facing them and their people in that part of Canada. I congratulate them upon the energy and sincerity they have displayed in presenting those problems. As one whose paternal ancestors were for six generations rooted in the soil of Nova Scotia, as one who has travelled rather extensively in that part of Canada and has, I believe, an appreciation of their problems, I do not hesitate to join them in their plea for simple elementary justice.
Many of the problems of the maritimes are similar to those of the great west. The maritimes are faced with an unfair freight rate structure; so are we. They are faced with lack of secondary industries and all that means, and so are we. They have their coal problem, and we have ours. They are faced with the fact that in Canada we find financial centralization in the two central provinces, which has mitigated against the proper development both of the east and of my section in the west.
I say to members of parliament from central Canada, you have the political strength here; but you must also have with that the understanding and the sympathy necessary to make possible the solution of those maritime problems, and also the solution of many of our western problems.
In that connection an hon. member from the maritimes stated only a few days ago that his people are beginning to look south. I say that in the west many of our people are looking south. Many of them-and I presume this is also true of the maritimes-have gone south, because of a lack of what they regard as proper opportunity in those parts of Canada.
In my estimation that is a dangerous trend, dangerous for Canada. I say certainly that if the solution rests within our power, then
fMr. Shaw.]	'
we must find it and apply it. I was astonished the other day to hear an hon. member refer to the 30,000 unemployed-and I am not sure whether they were in Nova Scotia or in the maritime provinces.

speechtext: The maritimes.

speechtext:
Even as applied to the maritimes, it is still an astonishing situation for us to view at this time. If one makes allowance for unemployment resulting from strikes, we are still left with a most astonishing situation.
I well recall two or three years ago, and more particularly just before the last election, when we had showered upon us those grandiose promises with respect to full employment. I am reminded of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), who, not long before the last election, wrote in these words:
Full employment is the declared policy of the government, and I for one am confident that as a nation we have the capacity to obtain that objective and to maintain it.
I cannot read those words with the same fervour with which the minister would utter them. Nevertheless, what he said is perfectly clear. And commenting editorially upon those words of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, the publication in which it was found said this:
Full employment is the declared policy of the government which means that work must be found for all; as the public welfare is the government's first responsibility.
In even more specific language, the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is reported as follows in the same publication:
1.	Full employment is the avowed and declared policy of the government.
2.	Most intensive studies and plans have been instituted in order that this objective may be attained.
3.	-
And this is the most important one.
-the most informed economic advisers are of the opinion that a policy of full employment is one within our capacity to achieve.
And that was written under this title, "What can be done in the name of war must be done during peace," and the subtitle is, "Public welfare must come first."

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But it is not full employment, or at least not my idea of it, when we find 30,000 men in a small area seeking employment, and even having to migrate out of that area in order to live.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is wrong.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister said that what they want is security. I agree. He said that they want a job to go to and nothing short of this must be provided, and that full employment is the pivot of the government's postwar plan.
I could fill the pages of Hansard with similar quotations emanating from cabinet ministers and other members of the Liberal party. I say to members of the Liberal party in whose constituencies unemployment might exist, you must be prepared to take whatever the unemployed are prepared to hand you; because you gave them those definite assurances. They cannot be expected to accept the excuses which some persons are so capable of manufacturing. Today labour enjoys its security, or semi-security as the case may be, only while engaged on the job, and only while in receipt of a pay cheque. I think it is recognized that if you stop that job, you stop the pay cheque, and you take from the individual everything, including his freedom.
Once you relegate the worker to that position he might well accept all that the anti-democratic or the subversive elements in the country or the community might be prepared to offer him. When the discussions respecting full employment were taking place in the house, and at the time of the last election, we made it clear that as an objective full employment was not necessarily the desirable thing. We contended that full employment, so long as it was useful and so long as it contributed to production so necessary to the life of the country, would have our support. But we also emphasized the fact that the only conditions under which full employment could be guaranteed would be those under which one would have the right to pick a chap up by the nape of the neck and throw him into any spot where you might find any kind of work for him. We find today a movement of persons out of the maritimes. I say they are migrating by virtue of economic compulsion. They have little opportunity of even surviving should they remain there and should conditions be permitted to exist under which they cannot find a useful type of employment.
I was interested in an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of April 18
with respect to this question of full employment. If my memory serves me correctly, the Ottawa Journal was one of those which gave a good deal of emphasis to the desirability and the possibility of full employment. Since that time, they have had either a change of editor or a change of heart. This is the editorial in part:
"Full employment" in other words, is a phrase that should not be used in a democratic state, this for the reason that it is something which can be practised only in a totalitarian state. Under a totalitarian regime, where men are told where to work., and when and at what, workers can be moved in the mass from one area to another. Under a democratic regime that can't happen. Because it can't happen, loose "full employment" talk does harm-may in come cases be positively mischievous.
I mention that for two reasons. First, you guaranteed them full employment; you built up their hopes and you have not given it to them. Second, we cannot have as our ultimate objective full employment when that involves the necessity of an individual engaging in useless employment in order to secure his income. I should like to devote more time to that, but there are a number of other matters to which I wish to refer.
Referring now specifically to the budget and taxation, I think to anyone who is at all observant there is ample evidence of the inadequacy of the tax reductions indicated in the budget. I know that to those whose taxes were reduced such reductions are welcome. However, there is one aspect which I wish to emphasize. Under the stress of war the government of Canada imposed a great variety of taxes, including sales tax and nuisance taxes, upon our people. Canadians accepted them because of the war and because of the requirements of war. However, no attempt is now made to make substantial reductions in them. In my estimation there is nothing in the budget designed to reduce the cost of living for hundreds of thousands of Canadian people. Nothing is to be found in it which will permit a higher standard of living for those persons who were forgotten by the income tax reductions. There is a tremendous surge of criticism in this country with respect to the action of the government in imposing certain conditions because of the stress of war and then persisting in continuing those conditions after the war is over. If my memory serves me correctly the Income War Tax Act was introduced during another war, and assurance was given then that it was only for the duration of the war and only to meet very special conditions which had come into being as a result cf the war.

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
In his budget the minister estimated government expenditures in excess of $2,000 million. As compared with 1946-47, this shows an approximate average percentage of reduction of nineteen per cent for the present year. I should like to compare that with 1939. If the figures which I have worked out are correct, for each dollar spent by the government in 1939 they now contemplate spending $3.80. The Canadian citizen finds himself in this position: for every dollar which he earned in 1939 he is now receiving approximately $2.80. The important aspect is that government spending has increased at a much more rapid rate than the national income.
The disturbing aspect of the whole thing is that while the national income may slip to lower levels, even to depression levels, government spending to a substantial degree has become fixed and will remain close to its present levels. It is recognized that, should a recession come in any pronounced degree, the government might resort to borrowing and debt redemption might not continue during such a period. In my estimation the real burden of the debt is the interest on the debt and the government feels morally bound to make those payments. We are already paying between $400 million and $500 million a year in interest. With a recession, with recourse to greater government borrowing, the burden of those interest charges might reach crushing proportions within this country. Interest is now taking between twenty and twenty-five per cent of all government collections. That is a tragic situation and, unless we adopt some other policy, we may find, such conditions as would block Canada in any attempt she might make to have continued stability within the country.
I know that this house gave very little attention to the amendment moved by my leader (Mr. Low) to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In that amendment he advocated:
The use of the national credit to meet at least some of the financial requirements for essential services; and, as a guarantee that this country shall not again be subjected to financial depression, to make available to each and all Canadian citizens a proper portion of purchasing power which shall not first pass through the usual channels of industry, this on a basis calculated to maintain a balance between effective purchasing power in the hands of consumers and the aggregate of the prices of goods available for sale.
I think it is becoming more obvious that in that rests a solution to many of the great financial problems which face this country today and which will face this country in far greater degree, I can assure you, sir, within the next two or three years.

I should like to refer to the statement made by the minister with respect to the revision of the income tax law. I have not as yet heard any reference made to this matter, but to me it is one of the important aspects of the budget. Referring to this, the minister said, as reported on page 2557 of Hansard:
We have been busy during the past year upon the rewriting of our basic income tax law in an effort to improve its arrangement, to make it clearer and simpler, and to remove ambiguities and anomalies. Hon. members will, I think, be particularly pleased with the extent to which it will be less dependent upon the exercise of ministerial discretions.
The minister then stated that it was his intention to introduce, during this session, a bill embodying this general revision of income tax law. May I say I believe that every thinking member of this house-I am going on the assumption that they are all thinking members-realizes the absolute necessity of a revision of the Income War Tax Act. I submit that, above all else, that act must be so constructed as to prevent the possibility of the extension of special privileges through interpretation. It is my conviction that, as the act stands today, there is every possibility of special privileges being extended to certain persons because of the regulations and more particularly because of the interpretations.
It should be borne in mind at all times that, even if the act is made perfect, its successful operation will depend upon two other things which I wish to mention. In the first place, it is my contention that adequate finances should be provided in order to properly staff the income tax offices. It is my opinion that you cannot possibly secure or hold the services of competent men unless you are prepared to pay them sufficient to make these positions attractive.- I believe that if the facts were known we would realize that competent men are walking out of these offices almost every day. It would be interesting if the minister would table figures with respect to the labour turnover in the income tax offices.
In the second place, unless they establish salary schedules in these offices and adhere to these schedules they are going to strike a blow at the morale of the personnel in the service of the Department of National Revenue, and I lay special emphasis on the income tax division. We all know that appointments to the national revenue department are not made through the civil service commission. I personally think that is wrong. I know that, as the civil service commission is at present constituted and with its limited authority, it works under tremendous handicaps. There is alto-

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
gether too much opportunity for interference in their deliberations. In fact, once before I brought evidence before the house to show that the commission had made appointments of persons who, to use a crude expression, were kicked out of the service because they were not acceptable to the person who happened to be in charge of a particular branch.
I want to emphasize this, too, that if there is any department of government where the door is open to the charge of political patronage, that department is the Department of National Revenue, and I say that because they ignore the provisions of the Civil Service Act. Let me make it perfectly clear that I am not making any charge. I am not saying that is the case, but I am saying the door is wide open. The employees they now have in that department must feel most insecure, and they can be made to feel much more insecure if they realize that their seniority and their ability are being ignored by the department. I do not care to say more about that at the moment except this. When the time comes for a revision of the Income War Tax Act, I say, by all means refer it to some committee of the house for careful examination. I would go a step farther and say, refer to that committee also the Excess Profits Tax Act. I should like to know something about some of the decisions made by the board of referees in determining standard profits. I should like to see that act and that specific section of the act considered by any committee of this house at the appropriate time.
Since my time is fleeting rapidly, I must leave out a number of matters to which I was going to refer. I come directly now to the amendment and the subamendment.
The hon. member for Peace River has already pointed out that, if the rules of the house did not forbid it, this group would move an amendment as soon as one of those now before us is disposed of. Our amendment would have been more constructive than either of those we are now considering. However we find ourselves in substantial agreement with the criticisms contained in both the subamendment and the amendment. Let me hasten to say this. I wish to make it abundantly clear that, while we are in substantial agreement with what is contained in the subamendment and the amendment, we are not subscribing to all that was said by the sponsors of these amendments. In fact we would be the first to condemn certain things that were said, such as the reference of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdon-nell) to the fact that interest rates were too low. I quote that only as an example.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member is one of the fairest men in this house, and I want to ask him this question. Will he be good enough to read what I said about interest rates? If he does he will find that all I said was that I questioned whether low interest rates were a panacea for everything. I pointed out that they bore hard on certain elements in the community. But as for advocating higher interest rates the hon. member will find that I did not do that at all.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should not like to attribute anything wrongly to the hon. member. What he said was:
Fifty years ago the man who retired with a modest competency could get five or six per cent on it and he could reckon on living the rest of his life upon the proceeds. What happens today when he receives three per cent? And he is lucky if he gets that.	_
I believe that when we are considering this matter of the low-interest rate policy-and I know it is difficult, though it is attractive from the government's point of view-when, I say, we are considering this low-interest rate policy I suggest that this very important factor be taken into consideration-it is very important indeed-that there are large elements in the community who are suffering greatly by that policy. One other thing I would like to say in this connection. I would ask whether we can go on freeing other things and leaving the rate of interest tied down tight. Personally I very much doubt it and I think it is a matter worthy of the most serious consideration.
If the hon. member says that he did not intend that we would' have to increase interest rates I am prepared to accept his word, but I read what he said very carefully and drew that conclusion, and I think the house drew the same conclusion from his remarks.
To turn again to the subamendment and the amendment, the hon. member for Peace River placed quite fully before the house our views on hidden and indirect taxes. No government speaker has in the slightest degree shown why there could not have been at least $50 million reduction in these taxes for the coming year. Such a reduction would have been quite possible without endangering Canada's financial stability or without running the year's operations into a deficit, even if the government persists in running affairs under the present antiquated financial arrangement. We would consider this a good start on the road of progressive tax reduction; this country would have witnessed an almost immediate reduction in the cost of producing goods and services, and the cost of living would have been eased considerably. The government cannot successfully claim that it is concerned about the welfare of the Canadian people in the light of its failure to do what obviously
The Budget-Mr. Shaw

it could have done to tackle the high cost of living problem. Therefore we support clause
(a)	of- the Conservative amendment.
It is our opinion that the best way to encourage the development of our natural resources is to take whatever steps are necessary to provide a ready market for the production from these resources at prices that will return to those engaged in mining, agriculture and so forth, a fair margin of profit over the years. The best market that we have for our goods is the one that is most neglected-the home market. It is quite obvious that there is nothing in the budget designed to expand and develop this internal market, and therefore our mining, lumbering, fishing, and farming interests are forced to scramble for foreign markets with all their uncertainties and problems. Therefore, with the second part of the Conservative amendment we must agree.
With regard to dominion-provincial relations, the leader of this group placed our position squarely on record in the debate on the address. Certainly this government has failed utterly to achieve unity in Canada and to secure the cooperation of all the provinces in working out a programme of social security, health, and public investment. It is quite evident that the concept of federal democracy held by the Liberal government is not one which makes for united effort toward a new order in Canada. Most of the provinces resent and fear the strong centralization tendencies which they have seen in the Liberal government. Most of them view with considerable anxiety the trend toward international centralization and the surrender by this government to an international authority of portions of our sovereignty, which action is bound to affect the rights and autonomies of the provinces themselves. The dominion-provincial conference machinery should be well on the way toward a complete restatement of the rights and authorities of the various governments in this country. Instead of that, what do we find? Ill feeling, division, and lack of united purpose. Under the circumstances, therefore, we must agree with the third part of the Conservative amendment.
And now a word about the C.C.F. subamendment. This simply adds two further parts to the Conservative amendment. With regard to the first, this group has consistently advocated increasing the exemptions under the Income War Tax Act. We think another step should have been taken this year. There is no reason why at least another $50 million could not have been taken off the taxpayers in the lower brackets, because it is perfectly clear that at the end of this year the govero-

ment will come through with another handsome surplus, one which they have no right to accumulate so long as the people are carrying the heavy burden of taxes which they are carrying. If we look at the matter from the purely orthodox point of view, something most certainly could have been done to relieve the people of the burden of this terrible tax. If the government could be persuaded to adopt an honest financial system, there is not any question about our being able to increase exemptions to $1,500 for single persons and $3,000 to married ones in this country.

The second part of the C.C.F. subamendment needs little comment.
