The house in committee on Bill No. 171, to incorporate Canadian Nurses' Association- Mr. Benidickson-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1 -Incorporation.

I did not speak on the second reading of this bill, Mr. Chairman, but I think many hon. members will envy me the privilege of being sponsor of the incorporation of an association whose merits are so well known as those of the Canadian Nurses' Association, as it has existed for some thirty-five years. The members of the association are the members of the various provincial associations, who, under the laws of the several provinces, become registered nurses. That group consists of 24.000 people and, after its long history, these people have decided for certain purposes that they would like to have incorporation by the federal parliament.
They publish a newspaper known as The Canadian Nurse, and in the course of their development there will be the acquisition of certain property. It is felt by the members that the time has come, after an existence of thirty-five years, when personal liability on the part of their officers and so on should be eliminated and they should have the right of incorporation.
The purposes of the organization are analogous to those of many other professional societies such as the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Medical Association, the national association that has been formed by engineers in the various provinces, and so forth. I could give other illustrations.
I should like for the record to indicate the objects as set out in the bill, which are those that constitute the background for the present formal incorporation in the Canadian parliament:
(a)	to dignify the profession of nursing by maintaining and improving the ethical and professional standards of nursing education and
service;
(b)	to encourage its members to participate in affairs promoting the public welfare;
(c)	to promote the best interests of the nurses of Canada and to maintain national unity among them;
(d)	to encourage an attitude of mutual understanding with the nurses of other countries.
Private Bills

The common and general terms under section (e):
(e) such other lawful acts and things as are incidental or conducive to the attainment of the above objects.
There is in the proposed charter nothing which in any way interferes with or encroaches upon the provincial associations that have been incorporated in the different provinces, or with provincial legislation. As a matter of fact, a prerequisite to membership in the national organization is acceptance under the provincial laws into the provincial association.
We all realize that the provinces are jealous, and properly so, of their jurisdiction, their provincial autonomy and the protection of civil rights within each province, and I simply wish to assure hon. members that, if each province decides that a nurse may be accepted within the regulations of that provincial organization, such nurse will in turn become a member of the Canadian Nurses' Association and receive copies of the admirable paper put out by this organization, which in turn will help to achieve the objectives I have enunciated.

I rise not to oppose but rather to support the principle of this bill, but I should like to point out certain aspects of the matter with which it deals. The promoters are all good people who are a credit to their profession. It took the medical profession of Canada nearly thirty years to form the Canadian Medical Association, and I know something of the difficulties that beset such organizations. I know something about the questions that nurses have to cope with, having been chairman, with the late Mr. Thomas Bradshaw, of the hospital commission in our city.
One difficulty of a national nurses' organization relates to contracts between employer and employee, property and civil rights within the province, and things of that sort. The situation in regard to nurses has undergone a complete change. If you applied for a registered nurse tonight in Toronto you would find it almost, impossible to get one, that is to say, someone who has taken the course. Moreover, hospitals have a great deal of difficulty in providing rooms. One floor in the big hospital in Toronto has been closed. The city provided the site for that hospital, and has very largely to help to maintain it with capital and per diem allowances. There have been large capital expenditures in connection with every hospital in the city; just the other day there was a capital expenditure of $250,000 in connection with a smaller hospital.
During the war a great many nurses went into the armed forces, and there grew up a
fMr. Benidickson.]
type of nurse called a practical nurse. What is a practical nurse? The common definition is that, a practical nurse is one who has just learned by experience, without having had very much training. They might have been employed as maids, or in any one of a number of other occupations, but they turned themselves into what they called practical nurses and charged $6 a day. Well, think of three practical nurses, each receiving $6 a day, together with free room and board and all the rest of it. No working'man can afford to pay that.
Then I want to point to the good work that has been done by the St. John Ambulance Corps and the Victorian Order of Nurses. I have no objection at all to the principle of this bill. I had a talk with the minister of health about it. I understand that he was somewhat opposed to it, but I do not know because he never told me; one of the members of the committee told me. Did these people, as promoters of this bill, ever consult the hospitals? Every qualified nurse is on a register, of which there are five or six in our city, and most of them are connected with a hospital. The promoters of this bill never consulted the hospitals, and as far as I know they never consulted the medical officers of health of the municipalities or the provinces. Formerly the provinces did not. pay very much attention or give much of a per diem or capital to hospitals, which were maintained largely by private organizations of one kind or another, and most of them with capital aid and maintenance of cities and towns. The city of Toronto made a grant of so much a day for each patient; I think it. used to be fifty cents, then $1.50, but now I understand it has gone up to $2 or $2.25. and in addition they have had. in the case of Toronto, to make large capital grants to all hospitals. Here in this parliament we used to spend only about $200,000 on the health department. Before the war that went up to about $475,000, and now they are trying to expand it still more. So far so good, but. of course it is impossible for this government to give anything to hospitals by way of maintenance or capital expenditure. The time has come when it will have to. The situation is serious for the working man, because he cannot afford to pay for this nursing service and hospitalization. For that reason the work of the St. John Ambulance Corps and the Victorian Order of Nurses is important. A medical doctor sees the patient, and then a qualified nurse comes once a week to look after him, at a charge of only $2. The Victorian Order of Nurses also did a great deal of good work during the war.

Private Bills
While I do not object to the principle of this bill, I think it might have been left over in order that some correspondence might be had with the federal, provincial and municipal medical health officers and with the provinces and the hospital authorities, because this is a matter concerning relations between federal and provincial authorities, which should be the subject of a dominion-provincial conference. It is one of the most important things we have to consider, because one of the first duties of a government is to look after the health, wealth, happiness and prosperity of our citizens. I do not oppose the bill; I have been told that the provinces have consented to it. But the provinces are not the hospitals, and I think the hospitals and also the medical officers of health and the medical schools should have been consulted. In addition to that. I notice that some of the incorporators come from other provinces. I want the bill surrounded with proper safeguards, and I want it understood that if this resolution passes it will not interfere with the St. John Ambulance Corps, the Victorian Order of Nurses or any nurse who is prepared to make her services available.

I am so glad the hon. member for Broadview is 100 per cent behind this bill. The province of British Columbia appreciates his cooperation and support. I think the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidiekson) made an able presentation. I happen to be an ex officio member of the nurses' association of British Columbia; and I hope that some time the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and the hon. member for Broadview, both of whom have an unenviable status, will come out and get to know the members of that association as I know them.
If there is to be any talking out in connection with this bill I give warning that I will talk out every bill introduced from every other province during the present session. I would only disagree with the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River on one point, and that is when he compares the high standards of members of the bar and of the medical profession with those of the nursing profession. I want to assure my hon. friend that neither he nor any other member of his profession can ever hope to attain such high standards as those maintained by the nurses in Canada.

I should like to say to the hon. member for Fraser Valley that the hon. member for Broadview has, in fact, been very considerate. He spoke to me before the house met this- evening; he had some
queries as to the status of the St. John Ambulance Corps and practical nurses, and I want to assure him and all other hon. members that there is no intention to interfere in any way with the status of those organizations or persons. I also want to say that the nurses are organized provincially, and that each provincial organization has seen the proposed constitution and has approved it. My hon. friend has also indicated some connection in an ex officio capacity with the nurses' association. I want to say it has always been a matter of great pride on my part that my mother was a member of the nursing profession of Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, may I first of all suggest that no doubt divorce legislation is farthest from the mind of the hon. member who is moving second reading, in the absence of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank). I am sure the hon. member would be the last to wish to have his name associated with this, and the following bills.
It is not my intention this evening to speak at length about divorce. I would point out, however, that on June 21, 1946, the then
Private Bills

minister of justice, in an effort to find a solution for this vexed problem which has been drawn to the attention of both houses on many occasions in recent times, had this to say, as reported at page 2713 of Hansard for last session:
I have suggested to hon. members of parliament concerned with this that there might be some other solution that would not set up divorce as a matter of right but would largely relieve parliament of the inconvenient features of the practice now going on. The courts of the province of Quebec pronounce decrees of separation for adultery. If parliament were to say, "We will not consider an application unless it is supported by a decree of separation based upon a finding of adultery," then the committee of parliament would not have to go beyond looking at the documentary evidence.
Since then I cannot recall having had any report from the then minister of justice, who is now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), with respect to his investigation as to the possibility of the solution he suggested should be advanced at that time.
Perhaps at some stage in the debate, or on some similar situation-and I raise the matter now because we have almost reached the end of the time alloted to private members-the Secretary of State for External Affairs would give the house some ideas as to the results of his investigations.
There was one further matter I wished to bring to the attention of the house. I had hoped that the minister, in collaboration with the former minister, might have reached some solution, because upon looking over the statutes for last session I find that almost a third of the space in that volume, which I now hold in my hand, deals with matters in which the average individual finds little interest. I refer to the 289 acts dealing with divorce at that session. From the point of view of the cumbersome nature of the statutes themselves, and indeed from every other possible angle, it seems to me desirable that something be done to find a more satisfactory means of dealing with a problem which in recent years has become so vexed.
I am told that divorce applications at this session of parliament may reach an all-time high. While last year there were 289, if my memory serves me correctly there are at this session already before the senate no fewer than 406 applications for divorce. I would suppose that before the close of the session those bills will have reached the House of Commons, and it will be expected that they will become law".
I have no desire to raise my voice unduly in this matter, nor have I done so during the

years, but I earnestly implore the government, through the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to do something in this matter. Perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs would speak to us concerning the possibilities which at that time he considered were bright, but which, upon further investigation, he may have found quite different.
I would close my remarks by asking someone in the government to take this matter up, to see if there is not some slim ray of hope whereby parliament may be relieved of this vexatious job which has been entrusted to it under the present laws of the dominion.

Mr. Speaker, I have watched the grave defects in this type of legislation, which we find in great abundance after every great war. The wives and children deserted are the ones who suffer. I suggest that during the recess the government or state should give consideration to that feature of the problem.
I believe that the Anglican Bishop of London, England, is expected to visit Ottawa shortly. Over there, for the first time in 350 years, they are about to change the divorce laws. A royal commissioner was appointed by the Archbishop of York, and some changes have been recommended. I hope the government will study that report. The right hon. the Bishop of London, Doctor Wand, recommends "reconciliation" and "forgiveness" as part of the programme. Reconciliation, he says, is a most important remedy and forgiveness is a healing force.
As I have said before, I believe county court judges could handle divorce more effectively, with cheaper divorces resulting. Judges of the high court are sick and tired of it. Before Christmas and before June, three or at times four judges must try divorce cases in the city hall at Toronto, to help clean up the list. The wives and children are the ones who suffer in these cases, and I hope something will be done about the matter. A civil registration system is also a remedy. Under Roman law marriage was a contract.
The royal commission in England was presided over by the Archbishop of York. I hope the government will study the report to see if the state cannot do something to relieve the great social wrong done the wives and children who are left very largely as a charge on the municipality and on their friends.

Mr. Speaker, if we were to allow ourselves to think of this list of homes broken up through misunderstanding we might come to the conclusion that it is a disaster for home

life in Canada. But when one compares this list with the list of fine Christian home3 in this country, he finds it is only a small percentage. I know of homes where young men were married before they went overseas. They came back, bought their homes and called in their minister who dedicated those homes. Those are happy homes.
I think we should emphasize strongly the outstanding number of Christian homes which are telling their own story through what they are sending out by way of clean character in our young men and maidens.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say only a word apropos of what was said by the hon. member who introduced the subject this evening. Anyone who has given thought to the subject must come to the conclusion that divorce has reached enormous proportions in this country. But I differ from the first speaker this evening when he endeavours to lay blame on the dominion government, either for the method in which divorce proceedings are carried on, or for the divorce actions themselves.
It is true, as he said, that the statute books are thick. I do not know how many members understand just how carefully the committee of the senate investigates every case which comes before it. I do not know of any court in this land which is giving more consideration - and serious consideration - to divorce, than is the senate committee. I am surprised to hear hon. members suggest that bills are being passed through parliament without any thought. Let us be fair in regard to the matter. Any hon. members who are in doubt can go over and see for themselves how carefully this work is done. There are those who speak about giving the senate more work to do. I am not a bit alarmed about the work they are doing.
All this does not touch the problem of divorce. This is one of the most serious problems facing this country. It is a problem which will have to be faced by the people of Canada, by the churches and by the provincial governments. I rose in case any thought was in the minds of hon. members that what we were doing here was condoning divorce or that no consideration was given to divorce bills coming before the senate committee. I think everyone will agree that as between the courts of this land and the senate committee there is more fairness, justice, consideration and investigation in connection with the work of the committee than in connection with the work of any courts in this country.

It would be quite illuminating to have a list of petitions for divorce which have been presented to the senate and the number of petitions granted. Back in 1944 the present Minister of Reconstruction and Supply' (Mr. Howe), then minister of munitions and supply, announced the government's intention with respect to a civil aviation policy with particular reference to the post-war period. One of the cardinal features of that policy was contained in these words which I quote from the speech which the minister made in this house on March 17, 1944:
Steps will be taken to require our railways to divest themselves of ownership of air lines, to the end that, within a period of one year from the ending of the European war, transport by air will be entirely separate from surface transportation.
That statement of policy was later incorporated into law by chapter 28 of the statutes of 1944-45, by adding a clause 14 to the Aeronautics Act. That clause provided that all licences then in effect under part 3 of the Transport Act, 1938, or under part 7 of the air regulations, 1938, should cease to be valid "one year after the termination, as fixed by order in council, of the war in Europe-"

I am not referring to the clauses of my bill, Mr. Speaker. I am discussing the principle of the bill, and I am reading from a clause of the statutes of Canada. The words I was just now reading appear in the statute, not in m>' bill; in fact, they are the very words I seek to have altered. That is the whole purpose of my bill. I will finish reading the clause: "shall cease to be valid one year after the termination, as fixed by order in council, of the war in Europe which commenced on the tenth day of September, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine".
There was another clause in that same statute of 1944-the act was passed in July of that year-which provided that, from the coming into force of that act, licences to operate commercial air services could not be issued to any company that provided transportation by means other than by air. That was clause 12 (2). In other words, the government's policy was put into statutory form by the bill that we passed in the session of 1944. Some of us waited for some considerable time after that for that policy to come into effect, and finally
Aeronautics Act

in August, 1946, I questioned the minister about the matter and asked when it was going to be put into effect and was told by him that the policy had been changed. When I first asked about it I was told about an order in council that did not exist, but we have been over all that ground before and I shall not cover it again. I want to read this one passage from what the minister said in this house on August 17, 1944:
Mr. Howe:	I said that the date of applying
the policy had been advanced one year 'by the government; and I was giving my own opinions, as minister responsible for the services, that the policy announced on that date was not the policy which would give best service to the public in the area. That is my own opinion. The government policy has not been changed, and will not be changed, naturally, until the act is changed. The House of Commons must approve any change of policy, because this house passed the act which established the earlier government policy.
My contention, Mr. Speaker, is this, that the house put into statute form the policy which the government had announced in March, 1944. That policy called for divesting of the ownership of air lines from railways within one year after the end of the war in Europe. That was the clear understanding of the minister himself, as he so stated. It is down in black-and-white in Hansard that that meant one year after May 8, 1945. Subsequently, it has been contended by the government that legally, for the purposes of this act, the war is not yet over in Europe and will not be over until an order in council has been passed fixing the date. That, in other words, puts off as a movable feast the time when this policy is to be brought into effect.
The purpose of the bill the second reading of which I now move is to bring some finality into this matter and make it clear whether this policy is to be put into effect or, if not, whether it is to be changed in the proper way, by an amendment to the Aeronautics Act. Hence the only change that Bill No. 21 makes is to take out those words to which I have referred as a movable feast and put in a definite date, namely, December 31, 1947. The effect of inserting that date in clause 14 would be to make that the final date upon which the government's policy announced in March, 1944, shall be brought into effect.
I contend that this whole question of our air services, particularly in relation to the development of the great new frontier in the northern part of this country, is an extremely important one. I contend that what is involved in it is not just a matter of the relations between private air lines and the publicly-owned system, but there is
[Mr. Knowles.1
involved the whole question of whether we are to develop our northland in an integrated and responsible way. For that reason I feel that we should move on to some clear-cut position with respect to our civil aviation policy. It is for that reason I present this bill to the house. If it passes it will take us out of the present position which leaves the implementing of the government's policy as a movable feast changing from year to year, and inserts instead a definite date for its achievement.

speechtext:
In the speech from the throne we read these words:
Once suitable financial relationships have been arrived at with the provinces, my ministers have undertaken to seek, in a general conference or otherwise-
And I emphasize those words "or otherwise".
-to work out satisfactory arrangements with the provinces in regard to public investment and social security measures.
The idea seems to have gone out that, once these tax agreements are entered into with the various provinces, as a matter of course social security measures are tied up with them, and that if some of the provinces hold out, social security is not going to come to the Dominion of Canada. Well, I have a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of April 23, 1947, containing the report of an address at Hawkesbury by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), in which he said:
"Hawkesbury as a thriving industrial centre," said Mr. Martin, "has a vital interest in the social security plans of the Liberal government. If they are carried out as we hope they will be, these plans will bring to the families of this community a greater degree of security and a greater chance of happiness and well-being than they have ever had before."
From that speech one would think that the Liberal government had a social security plan which would be brought in, and that it was just around the corner.
1 should like to take a few minutes of the time of the house to refer to some things that have been said by the various provincial premiers with respect to this matter of social security and these agreements. In the first place, the minister himself made it clear, when he spoke to the board of trade in Toronto some months ago, that the dominion government alone could not possibly assume
The Budget-Mr. Timmins

the responsibilities which are involved in the social security and public investment proposals unless it had these great fields of income and corporation taxes and, further, that there would be further responsibility upon the various provinces in respect of the raising of funds for these particular services. Then on Monday, May 12, we had the pronouncement that the province of Nova Scotia was preparing to sign an agreement; but it was made clear that the premier of that province was approving that agreement on the basis of expediency. He pointed out in no uncertain terms that there were a great number of problems still to be dealt with. For instance, this report states:
Although Nova Scotia was taking steps to enter an agreement, Premier Macdonald saw many contingent difficulties and criticized federal authorities for approaching the problem in a manner which, in many respects, had been "unwise and unsound."
"I say that the idea of separate bargains with the provinces is wrong, and that great matters of this kind should be settled at a general conference between the dominion and all the provinces."
"The proposals of the dominion government in their latest form leave much to be desired and the methods followed by the dominion government leave even still more to be desired.
That is what the Premier of Nova Scotia had to say. Previously, on February 7 of this year, the same gentleman is reported as follows:
Premier Macdonald said his government's nonacceptance of the offer was "a matter of principle." He said Nova Scotia had two major objections, the first being Ottawa's insistence on retaining minor tax fields such as amusements and pari-mutuels. "You might as well do away with provincial governments if you leave them no power to levy taxes."
On a previous occasion the Premier of Nova Scotia said:
If the process of the dominion invading provincial tax fields were allowed to go on, "what is the end to be?" he asked. Can anyone deny that, if most of the revenues which the provinces are to enjoy are to be paid to them by the dominion, the time may not come-indeed, is it not likely that the time is sure to come-when the dominion will begin to say what use the provinces shall make of these revenues? When that day comes there will be an end to provincial autonomy.
Then this is what the Premier of Alberta had to say. I grant you that these tax agreements have now been signed, but the fundamental principle, the fact that in order for us to have unity in Canada we must have an economic system that will work this year and in the years to come, still has to be dealt with. The point I am trying to make is that it can be dealt with only by the parties concerned sitting around the conference table with the

dominion, working all together in the interests of the dominion in order to bring about economic and social security agreements which will be for the benefit of the whole country. Of course the province of Alberta has already consented to sign an agreement, but this is what Premier Manning had to say:
The government desires to make it abundantly clear that such an agreement is in no sense a solution to the problem of dominion-provincial relations.
The proposed agreements do nothing more than provide for a redistribution of certain tax revenues under a formula which is neither scientific nor related in any way to the actual financial needs of the respective provinces. . . .
It leaves unsettled the whole question of constitutional reforms which are necessary in the light of modern circumstances, and does nothing to clarify the ambiguity that exists as to the lines of demarcation between dominion and provincial jurisdiction and responsibility.
Further, Premier Manning continued:
. . . before the problem of dominion-provincial relations can be satisfactorily solved, agreement must be reached between the dominion and all of the provinces on a basis which is voluntarily acceptable and on terms which all parties to the agreement regard as reasonable and proper.
Any formula which fails to produce this broad measure of voluntary agreement falls short of that which is required to underwrite the stability of our national economy, irrespective of what temporary financial gains accrue to individual provinces.
I do not believe the matter could be better stated than in the words of the Premier of Alberta.
Then we in the house remember that on March 17 last the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when we might expect the conference to be convened. Referring to the correspondence with the premiers of the provinces, which he said contained several communications relating to the circumstances under which the conference should be reconvened, the Prime Minister replied:
The conditions set forth there have in the mind of the government not as yet been fulfilled. I am therefore not in a position to say at the moment when the conference will be reassembled.
I do not know what the mind of the government is, or whether or not it is going to change its mind. The people of Canada, no matter what their political proclivities may be, no matter to what political party they may belong, believe that there is a duty and responsibility upon the government and the treasury benches to call that conference, and to call it as quickly as possible, in order that these problems may be solved.
The first meeting of the dominion-provincial conference took place in August, 1945. The

The Budget-Mr. Timmins
last meeting was on May 3, 1946, when the conference adjourned sine die upon motion of the then minister of finance. Mr. Macdonald, the Premier of Nova Scotia, was one of the most forceful among the premiers in stating that the dominion-provincial conference should be called again, as he put it, as a matter of principle and equity.
If I may refer to the correspondence on dominion-provincial relations tabled in the house, and particularly to page 30 thereof, one finds that the Premier of Nova Scotia is writing the Prime Minister under date of December 5, 1946, and, among other things, states:
The government of Nova Scotia emphasizes its strong conviction that a general conference between representatives of the dominion and all of the provinces is the only proper forum for discussion of matters so grave and so important as this.
The fact of the matter is that it has been suggested that social security plans are tied up with the signing of these agreements. I am sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is not in his seat at the moment, because I did wish to say that, so far as I can find, there are no social security plans under way at the present time. The government has no social security plans to bring down, and we are left entirely in the dark.
Last week the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) asked some questions of the Department of National Health and Welfare, one of which was as follows:
What expenditures have been incurred annually by the dominion government since March, 1943, in connection with planning and organizing a national health programme?
That is one of the things about which there has been a good deal of talk, and many speeches, throughout the length and breadth of the country. The answer to that question is as follows:

We are getting pretty close to home. But, as a matter of fact, $478.21 in 1946-47 for planning for national health services and national health insurance does not give us much hope that there is anything around the comer in respect of national health. So I am saying to the government and to the Minister of National Health and Welfare: let them take the house into their confidence in respect of this matter of national health insurance that we hear so much about.
In fairness, I should place on record the remainder of the answer that was given. I read again from the return filed:
The above does not indicate the amount of careful study and thought which has been given to this subject by many officers of the department.
Well, we have all been giving it study and thought.
Their salaries are not included in the above figures, as it is impossible to estimate the proportion of their time devoted to this work. A full-time officer is now giving his attention to studies in this field.
He must have just started, because his salary is not reflected in 1944; indeed it is not reflected in the last four years:
And the entire research division of the department concerned, consisting of approximately ten persons is at his disposal.
The fact is that if the government started a health insurance plan tomorrow they probably could not bring it into being-so I am told-in a matter of some five years or more. We have not the hospitals. We have not the hospital beds in any of the provinces to take care of any health insurance plan.
Only the other day the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) was despairing of the hospital facilities in his constituency. So it is in Ontario, as I know of my own knowledge, and so it is throughout the Dominion of Canada.
The only real progress that has been made in respect of preparing for hospitalization has been in Ontario, where the premier has offered $1,000 per bed to any hospital in respect of any beds which may be made available from now on in hospitals, thus leading 'the way for health insurance, or whatever health measures may develop in the years to come.
In the United States they are dealing with this problem more effectively. We read that within the last week Mr. Truman brought down his policy in respect of health insurance, and the first thing he did was to have congress vote a sum of S3 million to prepare plans for hospitalization facilities to be made available. In addition to that, he has asked congress to vote another $75 million to prepare institutions to work along with the plan.
We have nothing of that sort in Canada. I know of nothing planned up to this time in respect of health insurance. So it hardly lies in the mouth of the government to say that, as soon as these tax agreements are settled, they are going to deal with matters of social security. The people think it is right around the corner. I am saying just as loudly as I can that I cannot see it just around the corner; and I do not believe the people of Canada can, either.
As a matter of fact, the Ontario Medical Association seem to have stolen the ball in respect of this matter of health insurance.

The Budget-Mr. Timmins

Last week they met and prepared plans for bringing in a plan for Ontario which, in the long run, will be the forerunner of whatever health insurance plan may later develop in Canada. They got started a week ago, and the best brains among the medical men of Ontario are going to bring in a plan which they feel will be workable. As I have said, they seem to have stolen the ball in respect of planning for health insurance.
We had expected that something would have been done in the budget in connection with relieving indirect taxation. From time to time during the debate a good deal has been said on this subject. People may have forgotten that we have such things as amusement taxes, telegram taxes, telephone taxes, taxes on railway tickets, a sales tax, -a luxury tax on jewellery and a tax on toilet articles. On Monday last the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said in the house that the budget provides as far as posible for indirect taxation only on articles that are not necessities. There are taxes on tooth paste and shaving cream, and I think we have long since come to the conclusion that these articles are not luxuries. Yet we have been paying a high luxury tax on them.
It is my opinion that a start should be made toward reducing these taxes. If it is ever going to be made, this is the time to do it when national production is up and when money is freer than it has ever been in my lifetime. This is the time to start to reduce some of these indirect taxes. It has been said in another place that the budget is a hodge-podge of levies, unrelated to levels or any discernible economic theory, as the Minister of Finance has demonstrated by failing to do anything about it.
In an effort to find out how these various taxes came into effect, who was paying them, how much they were paying and so on, I made it my business to try to find out how much the married women of Canada were paying in taxes. We have heard a lot about the married women in business paying taxes, and there should be some relief for them, having regard to production. I inquired of the Department of National Revenue as to what taxes had been paid by married women in 1946, but they were not able to give me an answer. Then I made the same inquiry in respect of 1945 and I could not get an answer. Then I asked this question:
How many married women in the Ottawa taxation area paid income tax in 1945 in respect to salaries alone (as contrasted from those who paid income tax on investments), and what was the aggregate of the income tax so paid?

Here is the answer I received.
Statistics have not been assembled in a form to answer this question definitely either for the Ottawa district or the country as a whole but, as indicated in a reply to a previous question, arrangements have been made to gather such statistics in the future. However, as a partial reply, the department estimates that there were approximately 110,000 married female taxpayers in all Canada in the year 1946. Their salary or wage income is estimated at $1148,000,000 and the tax payable on this income in 1946 is estimated at $48,500,000.
I made it my business to follow that up in order to find out upon what basis this return had been given. I found that there were no records with respect to this matter. I found out that there are no statistics in Canada from which to give me that answer. The fact of the matter is that statistics have not been kept, and the minister who taxes the women of Canada has really no concrete material before him when he places that tax upon the married women. Speaking for myself and with some knowledge of business, I think it has been a mistake that the tax was not ameliorated with respect to married women.
As we know, a woman in business has an exemption of 8750 and her husband has an exemption of 81,500. If the married woman earns more than $250, as between 8250 and $750 the difference is deducted from the husband's exemption. If she makes as much as $750, the exemption of her husband is reduced to $750. We all know that the married women in business are doing their share. Probably your stenographer in the parliament buildings is a married woman. I know that my stenographer in my business is a married woman. There are nurses, teachers and stenographers who are carrying on their work in the Dominion of Canada, and it seems to me that some start should have been made in 1947 with respect to relief in the interests of production in Canada, which, after all, is one of the problems that we have to face. We must keep up production in order to maintain the supply of goods, and in order that in the course of time the price of goods may be reduced and that we may be able to get back to the economy of normal times. I think we might have had some leadership in respect of that, particularly since the minister has told us in his budget that he is budgeting for a surplus, I think he said of an estimated $190 million. He tells us that that is to take care of the agreements with the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

And to take care of debt reduction too.

The Budget-Mr. Grant

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And to take care of debt reduction too. It is perfectly obvious that in 1947, having regard to the start that has so far been made, there will be no dominion-provincial conference called. Since the provinces which have not signed agreements have balanced their budgets for 1947, I presume that the minister could almost put out his hand and find this surplus which he is to have for the year 1947. As a matter of fact, it may not be too late yet to take action with respect to some of the things that people have been clamouring for-after all, we are only the representatives of the people-things like soft drinks for the kiddies. Perhaps the tax on soft drinks could be relieved with the surplus the minister will have in his hands by the end of the year.
I obtained a return from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) with respect to taxes on soft drinks in 1946, which states that something like S17 million was secured. There was a tax of one cent a bottle and an additional tax of twenty-five per cent. I think the minister, with a surplus in hie hands or with a surplus staring him in the face, could have done something about that, as well as the tax on chocolate bars. In the same way, something might have been done to relieve taxation upon married women.
I should like to turn for a moment to housing. When the Minister of National Health and Welfare was speaking in Hawkesbury on April 23, he had something to say about housing, and I quote:
Under the National Housing Act we have provided more than $400,000,000 to assist Canadians in building homes. It is expected that 80,000 new homes will be completed by the end of this year.

industrial building shows an increase of 116 per cent. I think his survey should show him that, as a matter of fact, we are going behind in house building in 1947. subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes at my disposal I can refer only briefly to what has been said by the last few speakers. The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Timmins) seems to have become converted to a policy of social legislation, because he devoted from half to three-quarters of his time to social legislation and said that the government was very slow in bringing it down. In that respect he was somewhat different from the hon. member who preceded him, who said that the family allowance was a brazen bribe to the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), in speaking this evening, spent a good deal of his time in talking about the maritime provinces. That is an old political trick, .getting away from one's own part of the country and going to the other end to talk about unemployment there, when there is none perhaps in his own part of the country.
I listened to the Tory member from Queens (Mr. McLure). I could not catch all he said today, but I read in yesterday's Hansard how he began his speech last night. He referred to Marc Antony. I am not going to read to the house what he said. I would not want to repeat it because I am afraid we are getting on our hands in this house a case of senile perversion. Old fools are the worst fools.
He said that he was speaking for the province of Prince Edward Island. I want to remind the house that the hon. member was speaking for the Tories of Prince Edward Island, the minority and a very small minority of the people of Prince Edward Island. The hon. member also said that he hoped there would be a by-election in Prince Edward Island. I would remind him that if there is a by-election there it will not be a dual one like the last one he ran in, and he will not be able again to hold on to the coat-tail of another member to get into this house. That is how he got in at the last election, and he cannot deny that. His speech today bears out what appears in his biography in the Parliamentary Guide, which says that he was at one
The Budget-Mr. Grant

time a commercial ambassador. Well, all I have to say is that he made a commercial speech today.
I did think he was not fair in speaking about the fur business, because he gave the government no credit for saving the fur situation in Prince Edward Island this year. The government this year gave the fur men in Prince Edward Island a guaranteed price equal to the average price over the last three years, and saved the fur business of Prince Edward Island. My hon. friend and a few other men like him put the fur business on the rough in Prince Edward Island. As he was speaking, I was just thinking that the Tories must have had .a bet among themselves as to who could make the most ridiculous speech and, after listening to the hon. member for Queens, I would say that he won the bet.
When a doctor is called out to see a patient he keeps an open mind until he arrives at the bedside. That was the state of mind I tried to maintain the night the budget was presented to the house. My diagnosis of the loyal opposition, in their reaction to the budget, is one of shock, shock from bitter disappointment, shock from shattered hopes. I noticed that one or two of them, notably the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), who is of my own profession, seemed to retain their normal demeanour in the house on that occasion, and I decided that I would leave the treatment of his colleagues to him. I think he has made a very good job of it. Of course time is a great healer, and I notice that some of our hon. friends opposite have been coming back to life in the last few days.
I should like in that connection to rededicate a few lines to the hon. member for Lanark:
He listens earnestly to tales of grief,
Forgets himself, that he may give relief
To bodies suffering, or tortured minds,
In service to all men, his pleasure finds.
I have thought from the first, Mr. Speaker, that this budget did not need any defence. I suppose that some hon. members on this side of the house rose to speak on the budget in order to make their first speech. I noticed that one of the most sensible Conservatives in the house, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) overran his time, and he did not mention the budget at any time during his whole budget speech, which made me think that he had nothing at all to say against the budget.
This budget reduces taxation and shows a large surplus, and those are the two chief things about any budget. When we find

taxation reduced and a substantial surplus we are generally satisfied that everything else is fairly good. But the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), the financial critic of the opposition, seemed to be affected much more than the rest of his colleagues, and he made a confession to the effect that if his party were in power the people of this country would have to pay a higher rate of interest on mortgages and notes of hand and so forth which they owed to these rich people. He also said that if his party were in power there would not be any surplus, or words to that effect. That is about all that I could gather from his speech.
Every hon. member who has spoken in this debate has congratulated the young Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), not only on his budget, but on the splendid manner in which he delivered it, and I wish to join with others in extending my heartiest congratulations to him. I also wish to congratulate every member of the Liberal party, back benchers and myself included, upon the way we stood behind our leader through thick and thin because we knew he was right, and so I want to congratulate the whole Liberal party as well as the Minister of Finance on that wonderful budget. I also congratulate the Liberal party on the fact that today Canada is more prosperous than ever before. That has been admitted by almost every hon. member. Canada is the third trading nation of the world today. I remember that in 1930 Canada was the fifth trading nation of the world.

speechtext: What government was in power then?

The Tories. The excuse they gave was that there was a world depression. That is why Canada went down to eighth trading place in the world. If Canada went to the eighth trading place some other nations took her place. They must have been prospering. Another nation took her place and she went down to eighth place, et cetera. Today, under a Liberal government, she is the third) trading nation of t'he world. Canada is a country of something over ten million people. There are countries that have hundreds of millions of people, and yet we are the third trading nation of the world under a Liberal government.

The Budget-Mr. Grant
We hear many wails from all parties on the other side of the house about prosperity. Do they ever look at the reports of the bank presidents of Canada? These reports show that, in spite of all the money people put into victory bonds to win the war, they have twice as much money in the savings bank now.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: Including the C.C.F.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, including the C.C.F. They have twice as much money in the bank today as they ever had before. How does that come about in a country that some people are wailing about? Sometimes they forget and say that we are the most prosperous country in the world. Where did the money come from for the people of the country last year to buy more insurance than they ever bought in any other two years? Last year the people of Canada bought $1,777 million worth of insurance. Where do they get the money? Bennett did not send it to them. We are now told by our Tory friends, who have become socialists themselves, that we have turned socialist. If my hon. friend makes another speech like the one he just made he had better go over with the C.CJF. It was not since the C.C.F. were created in Canada that we had social legislation. We had social legislation in 1923, the Combines Investigation Act; the Old Age Pensions Act under a Liberal government in 1927; the fair wage and eight-hour day in 1928; the Farm Loan Act in 1926 and the Family Allowances Act in 1944, of course, and unemployment insurance and scores of other social legislation before our hon. friends of the C.C.F. party commenced to function.
Last year the Tory member for Queens talked; about the unemployed and jobless in Prince Edward Island. I said in the house afterwards that there was no unemployment in Prince Edward Island with the exception of some returned soldiers who had recently come home and were not yet rehabilitated. Well, there was an awful noise about that in Tory circles. The leader of the opposition on the island got up in the legislature and said that I was an outlaw, or words to that effect. I had said that fishermen were banking money down there. He said, the idea of fishermen banking money; the idea of a man talking like that in Ottawa. Well, I leave, it to him. That is Tory mentality.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman talks enough in the house. The hon. gentleman is very proud. He knows what Pope said about pride. He said:
Of all the causes that conspire to blind
Man's erring judgment, and misguide the mind,
What the weak head with strongest bias rules,
Is pride, the never-failing vice of fools.
The Guardian newspaper, which was at the time I think somewhat under the influence of the Tory member for Queens, came out with an editorial, and of all the lacings a man ever got for saying that Prince Edward Island had' no unemployment I got it. That was a year-ago. I am going to take time to read another ' editorial, because my hon. friend said' that Liberal papers sometimes find fault with; the government. This is from the Tory Guardian newspaper of April 17, 1947. It was nine months after I made my speech. The heading of the article is: "Our Island Prosperity" and reads as follows:
Annus maribilis well describes the past year as the prospects for the coming year. We have been free from catastrophies due to nature or man's making, and have enjoyed ideal weather, social, health and business conditions for almost eighteen months,-
That goes back a year before I said there was no unemployment.
-and are still going strong in this respect. Mr. R. P. Hartley, superintendent of the federal maritime insurance commission, with headquarters at Moncton, reports that conditions here are the best in the maritimes, with the prospect of having to import labour to help out when the $4 million wharf contract at Borden begins at an early date. Returned men have been largely absorbed in farming and fishing and other industries, while construction work, which is exceptionally busy, is taking up any employables available.
This is the place where our hon. friends over there say there are 30,000 people unemployed. It continues:
The farmers have benefited extensively by the deal in potatoes with the British government which will net them some $8,000,000 gross on last fall's potato crop. There are some doubts about next year's market for lobsters on account of the powers that be in Europe claiming that that delectable crustacean is more of a luxury than a necessity and its importation should be discouraged. However, at the recent fisheries conference here, taken part in by the Minister of Fisheries, Ottawa, and the Minister of Fisheries, Quebec, hope was expressed that any such embargo would be delayed for the coming year at any rate. The loss of the European market would necessitate the development of a more extensive outlet in Canada and the United States, and may entail the greater use of air express for the purpose. Which reminds us that air training and air traffic have become thriving industries in the province. One of the two new headquarters of the R.C.A.F. for the maritimes has been transferred to Summerside airport, and extensive building operations to provide homes for the officers and crews will soon be underway. Plans are also under consideration for running a new car ferry between West Point and Buc-touche or alternatively between Summerside and Pont du Chene, to take care of the summer
The Budget-Mr. Grant

auto traffic between here and tie mainland. This will be in addition to the Borden-Tormen-tine ear ferry and the Wood Islands-Caribou, Nova Scotia ferry which is developing a steadily increasing trade and traffic with Nova Scotia and Cape Breton; while the Clark Steamship service promises to be in greater activity than ever in the development of trade between Newfoundland and here. Altogether prospects were never brighter than at present for continuing and expanding prosperity in the garden of the gulf.
That editorial appears in one of the strongest Conservative papers ever published in Canada.
The opposition say that our people are overtaxed. Well, if they are overtaxed, why are they buying so many victory bonds; why are they depositing so much of their money in the banks, and why is it that, whereas almost everyone had to mortgage his farm while the Tory government was in power, there is hardly a mortgaged farm in Prince .Edward Island today? And that improvement has come about since 1935. I know what I am talking about. I am not like the fellow who said that there were 30,000 unemployed in the maritimes, the fellow who did not know what he was talking about. We had two or three major strikes on at the time and minor ones as well, and he was adding them to the list of the unemployed, and very likely adding the school children as well.
Let me mention one nuisance tax, an old Tory tax. I refer to the sales tax. We say that our dollar is at par, but it is not at par when you consider the sales tax. You cannot go out with a dollar without somebody getting eight cents out of it in the form of sales tax, and ultimately the consumer finds that he pays twenty cents out of the dollar through that confounded nuisance Tory sales tax. I say, as a Liberal government, let us as soon as possible get rid of that Tory sales tax.
I should like to say a word about the mail couriers while I am on my feet if I have the time.
Some hon. MEMBERS; Go on.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have heard an uproar in this house from our Conservative friends opposite about the terrible plight of the mail couriers. They say the condition of these people is a scandal. That is what they said a short time ago, and I believe they were expecting a general election at that time, because the same thing took place in the last session before the 1930 election. At that time Mr. Guthrie of the Tory opposition went so far as to move an amendment to the Post Office Act to provide that mail couriers should be placed in the civil service of Can-

ada, knowing that it could not easily be done. That was the last session before the 1930 election and, as I say, it was Hugh Guthrie who moved the amendment. Our hon. friends opposite made speeches then exactly the same as their successors have recently been making on the same subject, but I notice that it was the younger members who spoke. The old shell-backs who were here in 1930 did not speak. It was the younger members who put up the howl about the mail couriers, and they shed tears, just as their predecessors did in 1930. In 1930 that amendment was moved to the Post Office Act, but it was voted down. Then the election came on and every mail driver received a letter signed "R. B. Bennett", stating that if the Conservatives were put into power the mail drivers would be put in the civil service. In that letter they stated that they had moved in the house the amendment to which I have referred and that it had been voted down by the Grits.
I read that letter and I may say that it was dangerous to meet a mail driver on the road at that time. That was the time my hon. friend over there, the Tory member for Queens, was shouting on the platform, "Look at your milk cheques". Yes; I saw the letter which these mail couriers received. But what happened afterwards? As soon as the Tories got into power, the mail couriers began to ask that they be put into the civil service. The Tory government then said, "We will have to do something with those fellows", and they threw almost all the mail contracts out for tender in a body. Times were getting so hard that the people were starving and could not get a dollar. Bennett spoke then of sound money. He said. "This is sound money you are getting", but it was so sound you could not smell it. Well, these men lost their contracts or got them at a much reduced figure. I know a man w-ho had a contract for $1,100; when it was advertised he put in a tender for $450 and got the contract again, and it remained at that figure until we raised it to $1,100 two or three years ago.
That was what the Tories did to the mail couriers, and here they have tried to start the same thing again this year, but it did not work because some of the older fellows said, "You had better drop that; the mail couriers have good memories".
