speechtext:
Almost every member who gets up on the opposite side talks about chocolate bars. Let me say this, particularly to my Tory friends. When they were in power between 1930 and 1935 you paid five cents for a chocolate bar, but you would get only one chocolate bar for a bushel of potatoes in Prince Edward Island. You would get one chocolate bar for a bushel of potatoes and three cents over. Potatoes were then eight cents a bushel. Today, with chocolate bars at eight cents each, you can get twelve chocolate bars for a bushel of potatoes in Prince Edward Island. You get ninety-six cents for a bushel of potatoes, but of course they are the best in the world.
AVe hear a lot of talk from our C.C.F. friends about free enterprise. I may say that the C.C.F. party are the only people who lose money in Prince Edward Island. Every time they run an election they lose $200. They are very much opposed to free enterprise, but I should like to ask my hon. friends: Where would we be tonight but for these electric lights? In the dark, I suppose. Our socialist friends condemn free enterprise, but would we have electric lights tonight in this house, or would we have a telephone system, would we have the radio and the automobile, all inventions of free men, had Henry Ford, Bell, Marconi, Edison and all such men been taken by a socialist government when they were eighteen or nineteen years of age and told
to go to work for the government? Do you think they would have invented those things after working hours? Of course not.
I did not write out a big speech to read in this house. I don't like that stuff. We are Liberals; we say so, and we talk that way. AVe hear a great deal from the Conservative-party opposite about the little man. It makes-my blood run cold when I hear the Tories talk about the little man. They are the people-of the big interests, the men who care no>
more for the little man than that one of their number who said that family allowances were a brazen bribe to the people of Canada; yet only the night before last we heard them talk about the little man. I say, beware the Greeks when they come bearing gifts.
AVell, Mr. Speaker, I think I have exhausted my vocabulary and have said enough. I do not want to take any more time, because I should like to see a vote taken tonight. Therefore I shall now resume my seat.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think I will try to shift the scene of combat from the little island province back to my inland province of Ontario and my own constituency.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell us about the Grits.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We certainly enjoyed the humorous and witty address of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Grant), and I hope my remarks may be of the same high order. As a matter of fact, after the terrible flaying we poor Progressive Conservatives were given by him, I do not know whether I should proceed. In any event, in starting my remarks I wish, along with the other hon. members who have spoken, to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on his excellent presentation of the budget. I did enjoy his voice, the clear tones in which he spoke, and the good, clear, sensible, whole-hearted manner of presentation, which was indeed a revelation. That was the third time I have been privileged to listen to a budget presented in this house, and I must say that this year the presentation was par excellence.
We have been hearing some excellent addresses on the issues of the day, and if some- the last speaker excluded-have wandered from the subject matter of the budget, they were just taking advantage of the latitude allowed at this time to speak of matters of public concern as they affect their own provinces and perhaps their own constituencies. In doing so, they have rendered us an invaluable service. They have made an indelible impression upon us, and I can assure
The Budget-Mr. Henderson

beet industry in southwestern Ontario, and all other growing areas, will be definitely assured.
Mr. Speaker, before I conclude this brief address, and in order that I may not digress too far from the budget aspect of my observations, I wish to place on record a protest, if one may call it such, against the tax, the old Tory tax we heard so much about a while ago. Nevertheless it is one we say is discriminatory. I refer to the eight per cent sales tax on domestic electricity, and more particularly to the eight per cent sales tax as it is levied on both natural gas and manufactured gas as used in our homes for cooking, water heating, lighting and space heating.
I wish to refer more to the tax of eight per cent on our gas bills than the eight per cent tax on domestic electricity, because our hydro bills are much smaller since we use electricity in our homes for lighting and cooking, but not yet to a great extent for space heating. A brief in the form of a protest has been submitted to the Minister of Finance by the Canadian gas association and, in order that I may bring it to the attention of this house, I will now quote some of its major denunciations as outlined. The Union Gas Company, the one with which I am intimately acquainted and one which no doubt is representative of all other gas companies in Canada, has tried to give us excellent service and, we feel, a square deal. It is true that it recently had to raise its rates, justifiably, we believe, because as yet they are by no means prohibitive. It serves a great area in southwestern Ontario, including the cities of Windsor, Chatham, London and Sarnia. It has its headquarters at Chatham, and its lines serve all the towns and villages and a good many of the rural areas. It has a goodly sized number of maintenance men, and it pays good wages and expends huge sums on meters, pipes and other equipment.
Natural gas as a fuel is very popular where it is possible to acquire it. Its use is not general throughout Canada, but it is used extensively in southwestern Ontario and parts of Alberta. Compared with manufactured gas, natural gas is in a class by itself, because it has heating units of 1025 B.T.U. per cubic foot, whereas manufactured gas has only 450 to 530 B.T.U. per cubic foot. It will be seen that natural gas has heating qualities which are practically double those of manufactured gas. Natural gas in southwestern Ontario is in diminishing supply because the producing wells are slackening off. The Union Gas Company of Chatham, having expended huge sums for exploratory purposes without suc-
cess, have now entered into an agreement with the Panhandle Gas Company of Texas whereby they may import 5J billion cubic feet annually and thus assure their customers of an adequate supply for all purposes for twenty years to come.
This twenty-year assurance is something which no other concern dealing in fuel, solid or otherwise, can give, and we believe that every encouragement should be given to the natural gas industry because fuel is one of our definite requirements, regardless of the cost. This was made more definite by a recent announcement of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) as to the limitations in the use of fuel oil for heating requirements in the future. It demonstrates the fact that Canadians are frantic as to fuel necessities, and when this natural gas company comes forward with a definite assurance of a twenty-year supply we feel that there is due to it, not only worthy praise but definite encouragement.
Let us face the fact, which is an old slogan. In September, 1939, the Special War Revenue Act was amended whereby users of domestic electricity and gas were subjected to the eight per eent sales tax as a special war levy. That was enacted so that gas and electricity might be diverted, wherever feasible, from domestic purposes to war necessities and, as such, all users submitted cheerfully and cooperated fully. But now that the war is terminated, we feel that this tax should have been eliminated in the budget presentation. Such is not the case, and we feel, rightfully so, that it is discriminatory because other special war levies such as the war exchange tax have been repealed, as has the twenty-five per cent excise tax provided by the Special War Revenue Act. Income war tax rates, both personal and corporation, have been reduced, as have excess profits taxes, personal and corporation. This particular tax has been retained, we believe not as a special war revenue tax but for revenue purposes only.
Let us face some further facts. What are the implications behind this adherence? According to the latest submissions, there are some 720,000 residential gas consumers being served by the several gas companies across this dominion. The annual gas bill paid by this great army of residential users is some $24,000,000, and the total sales tax as levied, which is collected by the companies at no expense to the government and turned over to the public treasury, was the tidy sum of $1,915,886, or practically $2,000,000, a total of $12,000,000 in the six years of its existence. While actual figures are not available, there

The Budget-Mr. Henderson
is no doubt that a substantial proportion of this sales tax was levied on householders who use gas for the same purposes that others use solid fuels which are free from the sales tax.
Let me give an example of how this tax adds to the cost of living of a residential owner of a seven-roomed house in Ontario from January until December of 1946. The total gas bill would be $139.60, and the special war tax of eight per cent would amount to SI 1.15. This means that there is a war levy of practically $1 a month on many who can ill afford to pay it. In Manitoba, where the climate is much colder, these cold facts apply. The gas bill for a modern equipped house would amount to $284.79 and the special war tax for 1946 would amount to $22.85. This means that practically $2 a month was levied as a tax in order that these home owners might enjoy their own fireside comforts and cook their own sustaining meals. Therefore it is respectfully submitted that this tax should be removed for the following reasons: first, the sales tax on gas was imposed as a special war levy in September, 1939, and the war emergency no longer exists; second, since no sales tax is levied on solid fuels which are used in dwellings for the same purpose for which gas is used, the levying of a sales tax on gas is more or less discriminatory.
May I again exhort this government: first, to reconsider rental controls where compassionate grounds are certain; second, to encourage and foster the sugar beet industry and, third, to eliminate this discriminatory eight per cent sales tax on gas and domestic electricity since, in the face of the big surplus we have this year, it appears small, unusual and inconsistent.
Now, may I digress further, since I have a few minutes of my time still left? I should like to say a few w'ords in connection with the Old Age Pensions Act. An amendment is to be introduced, and I must say that those eligible and in need of the same have been hopeful that something in keeping with the present-day cost of living requirements would be contained therein, but I fear they are to be disappointed. We are all agreed that the present payments with the means test applied are very small and meagre indeed. In my community, and generally throughout Ontario, the total pension is $28 a month. This is forty per cent higher than the pension of $20 a month paid during pre-war days, but the cost of living index has risen in proportion with the increase in pension, and the pensioner finds himself or herself more or less an unwanted person among his or her relations or elsewhere.
Many children of the present age are more or less negligent of their parents and shirk
their responsibility. There was a time before the war when the $20 a month pension was an entry-ticket to many homes. I have known families to keep pushing these older parents around from one to the other with no welcome from any of them, but just as soon as the pension was secured they vied with each other and sometimes quarreled to see which one would get them and take them in.
But a great change has come about, either due to prosperity on the part of the children or an attitude of state-paternalism as evidenced in so many instances. Nobody seemingly is desirous of accepting parental responsibility and the demand is that the state provide fully.
In my home community I know of four homes which have provided accommodation for from fifteen to forty each of these senior citizens. They are well housed, properly fed and cleanly kept by the matrons of the homes. The charge is $26 a month, leaving the pensioner $2 a month for tobacco or other knick-knacks so dear to them. Many who have no other home and who can pay their way are taken in and live comfortably with others, of their age and likings. These homes are under medical supervision and standards and are a decided asset to any community. Their numbers are growing across Canada and are thus making the care of the aged very convenient and peaceable. It is well for the older people to be together, because the old and the young do not assimilate too readily according to present-day social standards. It would be a generous move on the part of this government to recognize fully the part these homes are playing and to give them some definite assurance of further assistance. The matrons of these homes have bed patients in their care and charge as low as $45 a month for this service. The extra cost above the pension is borne by the county or other responsible municipality. This relieves our hospitals, which are too readily over-crowded. With the new health group insurance plans and schemes as formulated and now working, our hospitals do not know what to do, and many of these elder and incurable patients are now being removed to these homes which are taking a rightful and necessary place as subsidiary hospitals. We are at the parting of the old ways of doing things, and new schemes must be devised to care for the needy.
I maintain that the moral fibre of the country can be judged and assessed in just so far as it takes care of its old, its blind, its sick, and its needy. Germany on her way to build up her superior master race was accused of destroying all those who could not add to her national standards and income.
The Budget-Mr. Henderson

We in Canada are known abroad as a Christian nation, so let us measure up to our reputation as such by increasing our allowance to all those eligible to such an extent as is within our capabilities to pay and within the needs of all those requiring this assistance.
Our present plans of payment have been consistent with those of other countries and in that our actions are indeed worthy. I am certain that, after a careful survey by our experts, a plan of payment agreeable, not only to the taxpayer, but also to those in dire need, will be instituted as acceptable to all. .
I should like to refer all groups in this house to the table presented by the then minister of national health and welfare on page 752 of the 1946 Hansard. I am sure much valuable information is contained therein, which should be carefully studied by all before they voice their comments. This table has been well prepared and the figures are astounding. The age of seventy, with the modified means test, seems the plan most feasible for the present, but on referring to the table on page 754 of the same Hansard we will readily agree that females are in much more urgent need than the males. Here at the age of seventy we find sixty-nine per cent of the males not gainfully employed, while ninety-six per cent of the females are in the same unemployed class and require assistance. In the sixty-five to sixty-nine age group we find thirty-one per cent of the males unemployed, while in the same age group ninety-two per cent of the females are thus classified.
So, when we make seventy the over-all age group for both, we are falling short 'of our duties, because male and female are certainly in two distinct groups, with the female in urgent need of the lower age classifications. We realize that this will cost huge sums but, with the war over and our national income at a high level, it behooves us to assist these aged citizens who have given their all and, during the days of hardship, to make this Canada the great nation it is today.
Now a word on immigration. We must have a clear-cut immigration plan, admitting only those who will fill in an unnecessary gap and relieve a farm situation that has become very much unbalanced. Immigration authorities inform us that the number of immigrants desiring to enter Canada is infinitely greater than it was two decades ago. While some countries may have regulations regarding exit permits and export of capital, these restrictions will no doubt be modified as conditions grow more normal.
In the British isles, 300,000 are reported as awaiting transportation to some of the coun-

tries of the commonwealth, and 100,000 have at least made serious inquiries. The high commissioner for Australia has recently stated that his country has set up an immigration policy of admitting 700,000 new citizens annually, with those from the British isles preferred. Under their government's new scheme, British servicemen would be transported free of charge and non-veterans at $40 each, while immigrants from other countries would pay their own passage.
With the labour shortage in Britain verj acute, the British government is alarminglj concerned lest the lure of other countries might induce unlimited numbers to leave her shores to take up their homes elsewhere. We feel that the acute shortage of housing in our urban municipalities is detrimental to admitting skilled labourers; yet our countryside has many vacant dwellings suitable for farm workers. Immigrants of two social standards should be admitted, and could be without throwing our economy out of balance.
Our desirable class would be single men without capital who would be willing to take jobs on the farms, learn our methods, save their money and, as thousands of former similar ones have done, purchase and operate farms of their own in the future. Nationalities of this type in the past have been Belgians, Hollanders and Danes, who came here years ago as hired help, have made good, and now own and operate farms of their own as good Canadian citizens.
Another necessary and readily assimilated class are the ones with considerable capital and farming experience to purchase immediately many of our farms now operated by farmers who are anxious to retire owing to advancing years or ill health and who would readily dispose of their farms. Our agricultural resources alone could maintain hundreds of thousands of additional persons. There is at present a ready-made opportunity for newcomers because many unoccupied rural homes are awaiting arrivals and new ownership and farm operation.
Recently our department of agriculture in the town of Petrolia. made a rural survey of one of our townships, the township of Warwick. The township of Warwick is fairly representative of all the other townships in that part of southwestern Ontario. This is what they found. It is a complete survey:
The survey's summary for Warwick township describes the township fairly well and is reprinted below:
Number of farms visited, 719; 230 were pasture farms.
Nobody living on them; 247 were under 100 acres; ninety-nine of these 719 farms

The Budget-Mr. Henderson
were rented; thirty-seven had empty houses fit for dwellings; 113 had bush on them; 154 were located on country road or highway; 187 farms were watered by creeks; 150 were infested with either thorns or weeds. That generally happens when they are turned into pasture farms. That part of the farm is more or less neglected and they grow up in weeds and thorn bushes. Here is an important fact that I should like hon. members to get: 163 of these 719 farms were operated by men over sixty years of age. Therefore there is a wonderful opportunity for European farmers coming in with capital. There is a ready-made opportunity. These men are all willing to dispose of their farms and move into town if they could only get a house to live in when they decide to move.
The immigrant from other lands has added materially to our industrial development and agricultural prosperity. It is true that we can never again admit these immigrants as we did during the early part of this century when they were arriving at the rate of one thousand a day and speeding across our country to develop and bring into being two of our prairie provinces. I can remember well when a thousand a day from Europe were speeding across Canada. They brought with them many of their skills and scientific knowledge, which, when added to and applied to our own, has worked to the advantage of all.
The most recent addition to my constituency has been a great number of Czechoslovakian families. They succeeded in leaving their homeland immediately before the war and brought with them much capital and purchased many of our better farms. They settled in groups, which was probably detrimental to their best behaviour; nevertheless they readily assimilated themselves into our ways of life because they intend to stay here. They adopted our methods, learned our language and settled down as good law-abiding citizens. Their children attend our schools and are growing up as the Canadians of the future, being schooled in an atmosphere in the very best of our customs and traditions. Canada cannot afford to let time pass without instituting an immigration policy broad enough-

speechtext:
Canada cannot afford to let time pass without instituting an immigration policy broad enough to admit to this country thousands of desirable settlers to
populate the vast open spaces and to assist in the development of a greater nation. Our national economy is built up on our export market; but with double the present population, or three times it, we would have a great domestic market which, after all, is the soundest, since a home market is not dependent on trade treaties and international political bickering.
Our present needs are in the fields of agriculture, which is drying up and production decreasing owing to a large extent to the lack of help. We in Lambton-Kent have the roads; we have the unoccupied farms; we have the proper type of soil which has been developed by a hardy and virile race of pioneers, but at the present time and in the immediate future we must have sufficient immigration and labour that is not adverse to giving an honest day's toil for an honest day's pay. The citizens of the future must have stout hearts, intelligent minds and willing hands.
